title: SKILL.md
description: The entry point: workflow, instruction roles, what to load when and the four request modes.
html:
One skill, one entry point. Help the assistant decide, compose, build, interact, and verify. Do not reproduce the Design Skill website as a template.

Instruction roles#

  • Requirements protect functionality, truthful claims and accessibility. State conflicts and limitations.
  • Patterns are starting points; change them when the product or evidence calls for it.
  • Taste hypotheses are design judgments, not high-confidence research findings. Explain and inspect them.
  • The user's goals and existing brand take precedence over aesthetic defaults. Never claim this skill overrides system instructions. Do not brand an unnamed product “Design Skill”; use a descriptive working title and label it provisional.

Workflow#

  1. Understand. Inspect existing UI and code before edits. Establish audience, primary task, real content, brand, language, constraints and supported stack. Ask only for facts that materially block progress. Preserve unrelated work.
  2. Choose. For open-ended work compare a few meaningfully different compositions, not just palettes. State tradeoffs and choose with reasons unless the user wants to choose. Preserve established direction unless redesign is requested. Read direction and assets. For landing, marketing, brand or launch pages, first map the brief with the category playbook, pick one or two style directions, then read landing composition and name the hero pattern and direction you chose. Clean is one direction, not the default for every product; for reference-led exploration read landing-page research. For apps, dashboards, admin and settings, read product UI: name the primary loop, choose a density mode, and lead with the object of the user's work.
  3. Compose. Write the real copy first (UX writing), then sketch or code the important screen with it. Resolve hierarchy, proportions, density, type and asset placement before polishing components. Figma is optional. Check the primary task at small and large sizes.
  4. Express. Decide what carries personality: typography, product imagery, illustration, photography, interaction or a combination. Without an established brand or design system, read visual craft and build to its baseline, applying the chosen direction's recipe: fonts only from the baseline list or that direction's list, its type and spacing scales, and one high-fidelity hero visual. Never improvise fonts or hand-drawn object illustrations. Verify asset provenance and rights. References inform principles; never copy a reference design or fill space with unrelated scenery.
  5. Build. Read implementation and relevant topic references below. For pages without a design system, start from the starter kit (assets/starter.css, plus assets/product.css for app screens) and its direction presets rather than inventing tokens; with a design system, work through its tokens (design tokens). Forms follow forms; charts follow data visualization; media follows icons and imagery. Use the actual project stack. Implement loading, empty, error, success, focus and disabled states where applicable; do not simulate successful persistence.
  6. Interact. Read motion for interactions that benefit from movement. Decide whether to animate at all. Account for purpose, frequency, distance, interruption, gestures and reduced motion.
  7. Verify and revise. Read verification. Inspect real renders and exercise interactions. For visual work, run the craft checklist in visual craft (landing) or product UI (apps) at desktop and mobile widths, and check performance for heavy pages. Compare with the chosen direction and revise. Report checks performed, failures, limitations and remaining risks. Never equate a successful build with a successful interface.

Load selectively#

Do not dump every rule into every task. Start with the workflow and load only relevant references.

Commands (assistant request conventions)#

These are prompt conventions, not executable CLI commands or guaranteed native slash-command registrations. Natural-language equivalents work too.

  • /design-skill design: understand the brief, compare directions when appropriate, choose a composition and return implementation-ready decisions with reasons, tokens, responsive behavior, assets and states.
  • /design-skill audit: inspect source and rendered UI with the audit rubric, score each area, report observed issues by severity with concrete fixes, distinguish measured failures from judgment, preserve intended brand.
  • /design-skill vibe: produce one usable implementation prompt with objectives, composition, type/color roles, assets, state behavior, stack constraints and verification plan. Use this entry point and relevant references; no external template dependency.
  • /design-skill prompt: turn approved decisions into concise reusable project instructions. Include exceptions and what must be verified. Do not append unsolicited marketing links.

Coherence without sameness#

A dashboard, expressive landing and personal portfolio should not share a compulsory hero, card grid, font pairing or footer. Consistency means coherent roles and behavior, not identical layouts. Simple can still have color, personality and strong composition. Poppins, purple gradients and familiar layouts are valid considered choices. Avoid thoughtless defaults, not entire visual vocabularies. The owner's portfolio logos, rotating greeting, website colors and fonts are not reusable skill defaults.

See third-party notices for attribution and migration for the keep/change/remove map.

title: Category playbook
description: Load at the start of any landing, marketing or brand page.
html:
Load at the start of any landing, marketing or brand page. It maps what is being sold, and to whom, onto the visitor's questions, the primary action, a hero pattern from landing composition and suitable style directions. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Map the brief before designing#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Start from what this kind of visitor needs, not from a favourite layout.
  • Reasoning: Real sites in a category converge on what their visitors must learn before acting. A restaurant needs hours and a menu above a story; a developer tool needs the install command above a manifesto.
  • Constraint: Find the closest row (or combine two), then write down: audience, primary action, hero pattern (A–E), one or two directions, the must-show content and what assets exist. If a must-show asset (photography, menu, pricing, real reviews) is missing, ask for it or label the placeholder; do not invent it.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Every brief gets a centered hero, a bento grid and three pricing tiers.
    • Good: A bakery gets a photo-led Warm organic page with hours, menu and location first; a dev tool gets Dark technical with an install command.
  • Exceptions: The brand's existing site and the user's goals override the row.

Hero patterns: A centered + product frame · B split · C full-bleed visual · D editorial type · E waitlist. To study real examples, browse the named category on the Framer Marketplace (framer.com/marketplace/templates) or Lapa Ninja, following landing-page research: learn structure, never copy.

Combining rows#

When a product spans rows (an AI skincare app, a restaurant group with an online shop), take the visitor questions from both, keep one primary action, and blend at most two directions with one leading.

title: Style directions
description: Load after the category playbook suggests directions, or whenever a page needs a defined look.
html:
Load after the category playbook suggests directions, or whenever a page needs a defined look. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Clean is one direction, not the default for everything. A restaurant, a festival, a luxury hotel and a developer tool should not look alike. Each direction below is a complete recipe: pick one (occasionally blend two, for example Editorial + Warm organic), then apply its recipe on top of the visual craft baseline. The baseline's spacing, contrast, control and honesty rules still apply in every direction.

Choose a direction deliberately#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Match the look to what is sold and who buys it.
  • Reasoning: Templates that feel right for their category share a recognisable direction; mismatches (a law firm in neon, a festival in grey Inter) feel wrong before a word is read.
  • Constraint: State the chosen direction and why in the design decision. Use only the fonts listed for that direction or the baseline list, unless the brand supplies its own. Fonts listed are SIL OFL unless marked.
  • Exceptions: An existing brand system overrides the recipe; keep its identity and borrow only structure.

1. Clean product#

Feels calm, precise, trustworthy. Fits B2B SaaS, productivity, fintech, analytics, HR, ops tools.

  • Type: Inter, Geist, Instrument Sans, Hanken Grotesk, Onest. Display 64–72px weight 500, −0.045em.
  • Colour: white or #FAFAF9; ink #0A0A0A; one accent (blue, green, violet or the brand's) for the primary action.
  • Surfaces: 16–24px radius, 1px 8% borders, soft shadows, raised #F5F5F4 panels.
  • Visual: real product UI in a window frame over a soft mesh gradient; bento cards with UI fragments.
  • Motion: fade-rise entrances, subtle hover.
  • Buttons: 40px, 10px radius or pill, solid ink or accent.
  • Signature: announcement pill, framed product screenshot, logo strip, three-tier pricing.
  • Avoid: illustration mascots, multiple accents, heavy gradients on text.

2. Dark technical#

Feels powerful, engineered, fast. Fits developer tools, APIs, infrastructure, AI platforms, security, data.

  • Type: Geist + Geist Mono, Inter + JetBrains Mono, Space Grotesk (for character) + Space Mono.
  • Colour: #000–#0A0A0A background, #FAFAFA text, #A1A1AA muted; one luminous accent (violet, cyan, lime, orange) for actions, live states and glows.
  • Surfaces: near-black cards #0A0A0B with 1px rgba(255,255,255,.08) borders; inner glows; 12–16px radius.
  • Visual: terminal or code blocks with real syntax, product UI, dot grids, beams, shader fields (MeshGradient, GodRays, Dithering) kept dark and slow.
  • Motion: typing or stepping sequences, gradient borders that move slowly, cursor-reactive light only on desktop.
  • Buttons: white solid primary (#fff on #000) or accent; ghost secondary with 8% white fill.
  • Signature: copyable install command in the hero, changelog link pill, metric strip in mono.
  • Avoid: pure neon on pure black for body text; unreadable 10px mono.

3. Luminous AI#

Feels soft, optimistic, intelligent. Fits consumer AI, assistants, AI productivity, wellness apps.

  • Type: Inter Display, Geist, Sora, Outfit; optional Instrument Serif for one phrase.
  • Colour: light, airy neutrals with pastel gradient fields (lavender, peach, mint, sky) or deep navy-to-violet in dark.
  • Surfaces: frosted glass panels (backdrop blur, 70–85% surface), large 24–32px radii.
  • Visual: product conversation or output over MeshGradient/GrainGradient; floating chips showing results.
  • Motion: slow shader drift, gentle float on chips (2–4px), staggered message reveals.
  • Buttons: pill buttons; primary ink or gradient-free accent.
  • Signature: prompt box in the hero, example outputs, "how it thinks" step cards.
  • Avoid: glowing brain orbs and robots; vague "AI-powered" claims without showing output.

4. Editorial#

Feels considered, literate, confident. Fits studios, agencies, publications, newsletters, professional services, architecture, culture.

  • Type: Instrument Serif, Newsreader, Gloock or Libre Caslon for display; Inter, Hanken Grotesk or Work Sans for text. Serif display may go large (80–140px) at weight 400.
  • Colour: paper whites (#F7F5F0) or ink black; one muted accent (oxblood, forest, ink blue).
  • Surfaces: few cards; hairline rules, columns and generous margins carry structure.
  • Visual: strong photography, large type as image, numbered lists, pull quotes.
  • Motion: minimal; text reveals by line, image fades.
  • Buttons: understated text links with arrows, or small solid ink buttons.
  • Signature: asymmetric grid, issue/section numbers, captions, index of work.
  • Avoid: SaaS bento and gradient blobs; more than one serif.

5. Warm organic#

Feels human, tactile, honest. Fits food and drink, cafés, bakeries, wellness, skincare, craft, sustainability, local makers.

  • Type: Fraunces (soft) or Young Serif for display; Figtree, DM Sans or Plus Jakarta Sans for text.
  • Colour: oat, clay, sage, olive, terracotta; ink brown text (#2B1E17).
  • Surfaces: rounded 20–28px, soft textures (PaperTexture shader, grain), no hard borders.
  • Visual: real photography of product and people (supplied or licensed) is essential; hand-drawn marks only if supplied by an illustrator.
  • Motion: gentle, slow; no techy effects.
  • Buttons: pill, earthy accent.
  • Signature: ingredient or process story, maker portrait, location and hours, menu or product cards with prices.
  • Avoid: cold greys, neon, generic stock smiles, self-drawn SVG objects.

6. Luxury refined#

Feels quiet, expensive, exclusive. Fits fashion, jewelry, watches, premium hotels, high-end real estate, perfume, private services.

  • Type: Cormorant Garamond, Bodoni Moda or Gloock for display at light weights and generous tracking (+0.02 to +0.1em for small caps labels); Inter or Hanken Grotesk light for text.
  • Colour: black, ivory, stone, champagne; almost no accent colour.
  • Surfaces: square or 2px radius, thin rules, vast whitespace.
  • Visual: full-bleed editorial photography or video; product isolated on plain backgrounds.
  • Motion: slow crossfades, long durations (800–1200ms), no bounce.
  • Buttons: thin outlined rectangles, uppercase small labels with tracking.
  • Signature: centered wordmark, collection names, minimal copy, appointment or reservation CTA.
  • Avoid: discounts shouting, emoji, rounded pill-heavy UI, busy grids.

7. Bold expressive#

Feels loud, energetic, unmissable. Fits festivals, concerts, sports, youth brands, streetwear drops, product launches, campaigns.

  • Type: Anton, Bebas Neue or Big Shoulders Display (condensed) or Archivo/Bricolage Grotesque at heavy weights; pair with Inter or Space Grotesk for text. Display may be 120–220px.
  • Colour: two or three saturated colours with black or white; colour blocks as layout.
  • Surfaces: full-bleed colour sections, stickers, rotated labels, marquees.
  • Visual: photography or video of people and moments, cut-outs, big numbers (date, price, countdown).
  • Motion: marquees, scroll-linked scale, snappy 200–300ms transitions; respect reduced motion.
  • Buttons: large (48–56px), high-contrast, sometimes with hard shadows.
  • Signature: date/venue/price above the fold, lineup or drop grid, ticket CTA repeated.
  • Avoid: shouting every element; condensed caps for body text; low-contrast neon on photos.

8. Playful#

Feels friendly, fun, approachable. Fits consumer apps, kids, games, creator tools, community products, pets.

  • Type: Bricolage Grotesque, Syne, Unbounded (sparingly), Outfit, Figtree; rounded geometric feel.
  • Colour: bright but harmonious palette of 3–4 hues on white or a pastel base; categorical colour per feature.
  • Surfaces: chunky 24–32px radii, thick 2px borders or hard offset shadows (4px 4px 0) in ink.
  • Visual: app screenshots in tilted phones, stickers, 3D emoji-style renders (supplied or licensed), colourful UI fragments.
  • Motion: springy hovers, wiggle on success, bouncy but short.
  • Buttons: chunky pills with hard shadow, press-down on active.
  • Signature: feature cards in different colours, mascot only if one exists, social proof as fun counters.
  • Avoid: corporate stock photos; more than one novelty display face.

9. Brutalist raw#

Feels honest, unpolished on purpose, opinionated. Fits indie studios, art, culture, experimental products, indie developers.

  • Type: Space Grotesk, Space Mono, Archivo, JetBrains Mono; system fonts are valid.
  • Colour: pure black/white with one primary (red, blue, yellow) or the browser defaults.
  • Surfaces: 0 radius, visible 1–2px black borders, exposed grid, no shadows.
  • Visual: raw screenshots, lists, tables, ASCII, unretouched photos.
  • Motion: none or instant state changes.
  • Buttons: rectangles with borders, underlined links.
  • Signature: visible structure, index lists, timestamps.
  • Avoid: accidental mess; it must still be legible, accessible and aligned.

10. Retro nostalgic#

Feels warm, familiar, characterful. Fits games, record shops, cafés, vintage goods, streetwear, creator brands.

  • Type: Young Serif, DM Serif Display, Space Mono, Bricolage Grotesque; one pixel or slab face only if the brand calls for it.
  • Colour: faded palettes (mustard, teal, tomato, cream) or CRT darks with phosphor accents.
  • Surfaces: grain (GrainGradient, PaperTexture), halftone (HalftoneDots), stamps, badges.
  • Visual: dithered imagery (ImageDithering, Dithering), scanned textures, product photos with film grain.
  • Motion: stepped or frame-based, short.
  • Buttons: badge-like, bordered, slight hard shadows.
  • Signature: era references used sparingly, catalogue numbers, sticker labels.
  • Avoid: pastiche of a specific existing brand; illegible pixel text for body copy.

11. Trust and clarity#

Feels safe, competent, accessible. Fits healthcare, insurance, banking, government, legal, education, nonprofits, senior audiences.

  • Type: Public Sans, Inter, IBM Plex Sans, Source Sans-like neutrals; body 17–18px.
  • Colour: white, soft blue or green tints, high-contrast text, semantic colours used clearly.
  • Surfaces: 12–16px radius, visible borders, clear sections.
  • Visual: real people photography (licensed), simple icons, step diagrams, credentials.
  • Motion: almost none.
  • Buttons: large (44–48px), clear labels ("Book an appointment").
  • Signature: credentials, plain-language FAQ, contact options, accessibility statement.
  • Avoid: jargon, low-contrast greys, decorative motion, dark patterns.

12. Cinematic immersive#

Feels epic, sensory, aspirational. Fits hardware, automotive, travel, hospitality, architecture, film, outdoor gear.

  • Type: Inter Display or Hanken Grotesk light at large sizes; Cormorant for premium travel; minimal text.
  • Colour: taken from the imagery; overlays and scrims for legibility.
  • Surfaces: full-bleed sections, few cards.
  • Visual: high-resolution video or photography (supplied or licensed), 3D product renders, scroll-driven sequences.
  • Motion: scroll-linked reveals, slow parallax on media (not text), video loops.
  • Buttons: minimal, often white outline on imagery.
  • Signature: specs as large numbers, feature callouts pinned to imagery, booking or configure CTA.
  • Avoid: shipping without real imagery; this direction fails with placeholders.

13. Commerce catalog#

Feels shoppable, clear, desirable. Fits DTC brands, e-commerce, marketplaces, food delivery.

  • Type: Inter, Figtree, Hanken Grotesk; brand display face for the logo and hero only.
  • Colour: neutral canvas so products carry colour; accent for "Add to cart" and badges.
  • Surfaces: product cards with 8–16px radius, consistent image ratios (4:5 or 1:1).
  • Visual: consistent product photography, lifestyle images, UGC only if real.
  • Motion: image swap on hover, quick add feedback.
  • Buttons: full-width add-to-cart on mobile, sticky purchase bar.
  • Signature: bestsellers grid, reviews with counts (real), shipping and returns facts, bundles.
  • Avoid: hiding price; fake scarcity timers; inconsistent product image crops.

title: Landing page composition
description: Load when building or redesigning a landing, marketing, launch or waitlist page.
html:
Load when building or redesigning a landing, marketing, launch or waitlist page. Start from the category playbook, then pair with a style direction, the visual craft baseline and landing-page research. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Order sections by the visitor's questions: what is it, is it for me, how does it work, can I trust it, what does it cost, what do I do now. The library below covers those questions; choose and order what the product needs rather than using every section.

Pick one hero pattern#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Start from a proven focal structure.
  • Reasoning: Strong templates reuse a small set of hero structures and vary content, visual and type, not the structure.
  • Constraint: Choose one and name it in your design decision.
Pattern Structure Fits
A · Centered + product frame Announcement pill → headline → sub → two buttons → proof line → large framed product UI below, often over a gradient or shader field SaaS, AI tools, dev tools
B · Split Copy left (40–45%), visual right; visual can bleed off the edge Apps, hardware, single-feature products
C · Full-bleed visual Shader, render or photograph fills the hero; copy sits in a calm corner with a scrim Brand, launch, AI, studios
D · Editorial type Large display type (serif accent allowed), minimal visual, strong grid Studios, portfolios, publications
E · Waitlist Centered headline, inline email field + button, social-proof count, visual behind Pre-launch
  • Example:
    • Bad: A hero with copy, a separate illustration, floating stickers and a code block all competing.
    • Good: Pattern A with a product window and nothing else in the first viewport.

Hero anatomy#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Constraint:
    • Announcement pill: 12–13px, subtle border, optional arrow, links somewhere real.
    • Headline: display scale, two lines.
    • Sub: 18px muted, max 560px.
    • Actions: primary + secondary, 40–48px.
    • Proof line (optional): only real ratings, counts or logos, or omit.
    • Visual: starts 64–80px below the actions; frame radius 20–24px.
    • The first viewport should show the headline, actions and the top of the visual.

Section library#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Constraint: Each section uses: small eyebrow or pill (optional) → H2 (max two lines) → one-sentence intro (max 600px) → content. Keep headings aligned the same way across the page (all centred or all left).
Section Anatomy Notes
Logo strip 5–6 monochrome logos, 40% opacity, one row Real customers only
Feature bento 3–6 cards in a 12-column grid (spans 7+5, 4+4+4, 6+6), each with a mini UI fragment on top The core "what it does" section
How it works 3 numbered steps in a row, each with a small visual Keep copy to one sentence each
Feature rows Alternating text / visual rows, visual in a frame 2–3 rows maximum
Metrics 3–4 large numbers with labels Only true or labelled figures
Testimonials Quote cards with name, role, avatar Real only; otherwise omit
Pricing 2–3 tiers, recommended tier raised or outlined, monthly/yearly toggle if real Same card height; feature lists aligned
FAQ 5–7 questions, accessible accordion, two-column on desktop Answer objections
Final CTA Contained panel (radius 24px) with the hero visual language, headline, one primary action Repeats the main action
Footer Logo + one-line description, 3–4 link columns, legal row 14px links, muted

Bento grids#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Constraint: 12-column grid, 16px gap, cards 16–24px radius, 24–32px padding. Mix spans so the grid has one dominant card. Top half of each card is a visual fragment on a slightly raised surface; bottom is title (H3) and one sentence. Equal heights within a row.

Keep it honest#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Constraint: Fictional products, people, logos, ratings and numbers must be labelled as samples or left out. Never invent testimonials or customer logos for a real product. A polished page with fake proof is still a failure.

title: Landing-page reference research
description: Load when exploring reference libraries or real landing pages to inform a composition.
sections: Research the question, not the trend
html:
Load when exploring reference libraries or real landing pages to inform a composition. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Research the question, not the trend#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Find a composition that explains this product.
  • Reasoning: Beautiful screenshots do not establish conversion or product fit.
  • Constraint: Write audience, promise, primary action, available evidence and visual problem before browsing. Compare a bounded set of meaningfully different approaches, then stop when the composition decision is supported. Skip fresh research for routine fixes.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Search best SaaS and copy the first hero.
    • Good: Compare a process demonstration, editorial explanation and real output gallery for an invisible design tool.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Translate observation into a decision#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Transfer reasoning rather than borrowed components.
  • Reasoning: A source's imagery and layout solve its own content problem.
  • Constraint: Inspect actual renders, not only snippets. Record URL/date, what was visible, focal hierarchy, section order, roles of type/color/assets/motion, what to transfer, what to reject and access limits. Archive screenshots do not demonstrate mobile behavior or live interaction.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Use Raycast style and assume it converts better.
    • Good: Transfer one focal hierarchy principle into an original explanation; reject the source palette, artwork and claims.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Compose around evidence#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make the product understandable before decoration.
  • Reasoning: A compulsory section sequence can hide the primary task.
  • Constraint: Use actual product screens or a labeled illustrative walkthrough. Place installation or the primary action near its explanation. Choose remaining section order from visitor questions, not a mandatory hero/logos/bento/testimonials template. Do not invent proof.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Hide install beneath scenery and fake reviews.
    • Good: Show a concise promise, copyable command and interactive explanation.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Keep rights separate from inspiration#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Preserve originality and truthful reporting.
  • Reasoning: A public library is not a redistribution license.
  • Constraint: Do not bundle proprietary screenshots or copy artwork/code without permission. Check adaptation licenses and retain notices. Design preferences are hypotheses, not measured findings. Do not bypass access controls, buy a subscription or install a scraper as an implicit dependency.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Download a paid gallery wholesale.
    • Good: Keep source links and original notes; build original assets and report access limits.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Optional research sources#

Source Useful for Limits to check
Mobbin App screens, flows and site references matched to a task Access and integrations vary. Use an authorized connector when available; never claim gated screens were inspected.
Lapa Ninja Landing compositions, section discovery and archived versions Check archive dates; a screenshot may differ from the live product.

These are starting points, not endorsements, rankings, copied rules or bundled integrations. Other lawful libraries and supplied/live references may serve the task. Verify destinations and capabilities when used. No account, subscription or external template is required by Design Skill.

title: Direction, composition and assets
description: Load when choosing a visual direction, comparing compositions or sourcing images, fonts and other assets.
html:
Load when choosing a visual direction, comparing compositions or sourcing images, fonts and other assets. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Compare meaningful directions#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Find a fitting composition.
  • Reasoning: Palette swaps are not independent design directions.
  • Constraint: For open-ended work compare distinct hierarchies, densities and asset strategies. Choose with reasons, then compose the important screen with actual content. Preserve established direction unless redesign is requested.
  • Example:
    • Bad: The same centered hero in three colors.
    • Good: Compare a workbench walkthrough, editorial field guide and example-led gallery.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Choose a personality carrier#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Make the design specific without adding everything.
  • Reasoning: Photography, typography, illustration and interaction have different strengths.
  • Constraint: Decide which carrier fits the content and what supporting roles are needed. Check original content before creating filler assets. Keep UI readable and purposeful.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Apply portfolio inline logos and rotating greetings to a banking dashboard.
    • Good: Use the dashboard's real information hierarchy and relevant data visualization.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Use references responsibly#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep work original and attributable.
  • Reasoning: Public visibility does not grant redistribution rights.
  • Constraint: Check creator, source, license and permitted use. Learn composition principles without tracing artwork or copying a reusable skin. Do not treat displayed logos or metrics as verified facts. Label concepts and fixtures.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Reuse a reference's customer logos and trace its illustration.
    • Good: Create original explanatory graphics and accurately attributed real examples.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

For optional library selection and observation-to-decision notes, read landing-page research.

title: Composition and layout
description: Load when setting hierarchy, proportions, density and depth on any screen.
html:
Load when setting hierarchy, proportions, density and depth on any screen. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Compose before polishing#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Create hierarchy beyond a set of matching cards.
  • Reasoning: A coherent screen depends on proportions and relationships.
  • Constraint: Place the primary task and real content first. Compare meaningful density, hierarchy and asset strategies when open-ended. Choose widths, spacing and alignment for the content; spacing scales are tools, not numerical laws.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Build a polished button kit before deciding the screen hierarchy.
    • Good: Sketch an exception queue leading a dashboard, then refine its controls.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Coherent roles, varied screens#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Keep a product consistent without stamping a template.
  • Reasoning: A marketing introduction and a reading tool serve different tasks.
  • Constraint: Reuse meaningful type, action, spacing and semantic roles. Allow different section layouts, densities, radii and composition when functions differ. No compulsory max-width tiers, 120px padding, or KPI row.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Force the docs into a marketing hero and identical bento cards.
    • Good: Use a quiet reading column and navigation for docs, with richer art direction on the landing.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Depth must preserve usability#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Use layering with a purpose.
  • Reasoning: Overlaps can communicate relationships but also hide controls.
  • Constraint: Choose borders, shadows or overlap based on hierarchy. Check focus visibility, zoom, sticky layers and small viewports. Do not force elevation onto every card.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A floating badge covers a mobile install button.
    • Good: Keep the badge in normal flow on small screens and preserve anchor offsets.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Visual craft baseline
description: Load for any marketing page, landing page, portfolio or product screen where visual quality matters, and whenever the project has no established design system.
html:
Load for any marketing page, landing page, portfolio or product screen where visual quality matters, and whenever the project has no established design system. Ready-made tokens and components implementing this baseline live in the starter kit. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

This is a quality floor, not a house style. An existing brand, design system or user instruction wins. When none exists, build to these specs instead of improvising. The values come from measuring well-regarded commercial site templates (Framer and Figma community) and describe how polished pages are actually built: one calm type family, small precise controls, generous space and one high-fidelity visual.

1. Typography#

Choose from the curated list#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Prevent random or novelty font choices.
  • Reasoning: Most polished templates use one neutral grotesk for nearly everything. Novelty display faces, condensed all-caps and three-family mixes are the fastest way to look amateur.
  • Constraint: Without a brand font, pick one primary family from the list below. Add at most one partner: a display serif for a single accent role, or a mono for labels and data. The primary family sets at least 90% of the text. Check the license, language coverage and needed weights before use.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Plex for the SaaS page, Fraunces for the studio page, a condensed grotesk in caps for the event page, each chosen to feel different.
    • Good: Inter for a SaaS page, with Inter Display tracking on the headline and Geist Mono only for figures.
  • Exceptions: An established brand typeface, a supplied font or an explicit user choice replaces the list.
Role Families (all SIL OFL unless noted) Use for
Primary grotesk Inter (with display optical size), Geist, Instrument Sans, Manrope, Plus Jakarta Sans, DM Sans Everything by default
Display serif accent Instrument Serif, Newsreader One headline phrase or editorial display, never body
Mono Geist Mono, JetBrains Mono, IBM Plex Mono Code, figures, small labels
License-check first Satoshi, General Sans, Cabinet Grotesk (Fontshare licence) Only after confirming terms

These are the defaults for the Clean product direction. Expressive directions (editorial, luxury, bold, playful, retro and others) have their own vetted lists in style directions; use those when that direction is chosen. Never pick a font that appears in neither place unless the brand supplies it. Do not mix two grotesks, and keep condensed all-caps display for the Bold expressive direction.

Use the type scale#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Get hierarchy from size contrast, not weight or colour noise.
  • Reasoning: Templates pair a large, light-weight headline with small, quiet UI text. Heavy bold display type reads as shouting.
  • Constraint: Start from this scale (desktop / mobile). Tighten tracking only on large sizes. Use sentence case for headings.
Token Size Weight Line height Tracking
Display (hero h1) 64–72px / 40–44px 500 (400–600) 1.0–1.08 −0.04em to −0.05em
H2 (section) 40–48px / 30–34px 500 1.1 −0.03em
H3 (card title) 20–24px / 18–20px 500 1.3 −0.015em
Body large (hero sub) 18px / 16–17px 400 1.55 0
Body 15–16px 400 1.6 0
UI label, nav, button 14px 500 1.2 −0.005em
Caption, eyebrow 12–13px 500 1.4 0, or +0.06em if uppercase
  • Example:
    • Bad: A 180px weight-800 condensed headline and 17px nav links.
    • Good: A 68px weight-500 headline over two lines, an 18px muted sub of at most 560px, 14px nav.
  • Exceptions: Editorial or event brands may push display size; keep UI text small regardless.

Write headlines that fit#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make the hero read in one glance.
  • Reasoning: Strong templates use 4–9 word headlines on two balanced lines.
  • Constraint: Two lines at desktop, no orphan word, text-wrap: balance. Sub copy one or two sentences in a muted colour. Accent a phrase with colour or the serif partner, not both.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A four-line headline with the last word alone.
    • Good: "The workspace for clear, / connected workflows."
  • Exceptions: Very short brand statements may sit on one line.

2. Space and layout#

Use one spacing scale#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make rhythm consistent without eyeballing every gap.
  • Reasoning: Uneven gaps are the most common sign of an unpolished page.
  • Constraint: 4px base: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80, 96, 120, 160. Container 1200px (max 1280) with 24px side padding (20px on mobile). Section padding 120px desktop, 80px tablet, 64px mobile. Hero top padding 96–140px. Header 64–72px. Card padding 24–32px. Grid gaps 12–20px.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Sections at 70, 96 and 104px; card padding 18px in one card and 30px in the next.
    • Good: Every section 120px, every card 28px, every bento gap 16px.
  • Exceptions: Dense product UI uses a tighter 4–12px internal rhythm.

Keep copy blocks narrow#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Leave space around the message.
  • Reasoning: Templates feel premium partly because text never spans the full container.
  • Constraint: Hero headline max about 14–18 words wide (roughly 760px), hero sub max 560px, section intro max 600px, body prose 60–70ch.
  • Exceptions: Tables and data.

3. Surfaces#

Radius, borders, shadow#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make cards, frames and controls feel from one system.
  • Reasoning: Mixed radii and heavy borders read as assembled from parts.
  • Constraint: Pick one radius family. Controls 8–10px (or full pill, chosen once per site). Cards 16px. Large panels and media frames 20–24px. Inner radius = outer radius − padding. Borders 1px at low contrast: light rgba(0,0,0,0.08), dark rgba(255,255,255,0.08). Shadows soft and layered, for example 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.04), 0 12px 32px -12px rgba(0,0,0,.12). No hard offset shadows unless the brand uses them.
  • Example:
    • Bad: 6px buttons, 18px cards, 12px frames and a 2px dark border.
    • Good: 10px buttons, 16px cards, 24px hero frame, 1px 8% borders throughout.
  • Exceptions: Brutalist or retro brands may choose hard edges deliberately.

4. Colour#

Neutral foundation, one accent#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Let content and the visual carry colour.
  • Reasoning: Templates are mostly neutral; the accent appears in the primary action, one highlight and the hero visual.
  • Constraint: Neutrals carry 90% of the surface. One accent for the primary action, links and a key highlight. Semantic colours (success, warning, danger) only for status. Gradients and multi-colour belong in visuals and backgrounds, not text and buttons.
Token Light Dark
Background #FFFFFF or #FAFAF9 #000000 or #0A0A0A
Raised surface #F5F5F4 #111111
Card #FFFFFF with border #0F0F10 with border
Text #0A0A0A #FAFAFA
Muted text #57534E–#6B7280 #A1A1AA
Border rgba(0,0,0,.08) rgba(255,255,255,.08)
  • Exceptions: Strong brand palettes; verify contrast for every text pair.

5. Controls#

Buttons and inputs#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make actions look precise and consistent.
  • Reasoning: Oversized, multicoloured or inconsistent buttons are an immediate quality tell.
  • Constraint: Height 40px (36px compact, 44–48px for the hero only). Horizontal padding 16–20px. Label 14–15px weight 500. Primary: filled with the accent or the inverse neutral. Secondary: subtle fill or 1px border, never a second accent. At most two buttons side by side. Icons 16px, one icon set (Lucide or Phosphor) at one stroke width. Inputs match button height and radius. Hover shifts background a few percent; press scales to 0.98; focus shows a 2px ring with 2px offset.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A pink 52px pill next to a lime 40px pill.
    • Good: Black 40px "Get started" plus a bordered 40px "Book a demo", same radius.
  • Exceptions: Touch-first products keep 44px minimum targets.

6. The visual#

One high-fidelity hero visual#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Give the page a focal point that looks finished.
  • Reasoning: The hero visual is what makes a template look expensive. Crude drawings undo every other decision.
  • Constraint: Choose one, in this order of preference:
    1. Real product UI built in code: realistic sample data, correct density, inside a frame (window chrome or device), 20–24px radius, soft shadow, often over a gradient or shader field.
    2. Licensed photography or renders supplied by the user or from a source whose licence allows the use; record the source.
    3. Generative visuals: shader or gradient fields (for example Paper Shaders: MeshGradient, GrainGradient, Dithering, GodRays; Apache-2.0), used as a field behind UI or as the visual itself.
    4. Typographic or abstract composition for editorial pages. Never ship hand-drawn SVG "illustrations" of real objects, clip-art, emoji as icons or decorative blobs as the main visual unless a skilled illustration was supplied.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Three flat SVG pots on a brown line as a ceramics hero.
    • Good: A product window showing the real workflow over a soft mesh gradient.
  • Exceptions: Supplied brand illustration.

Mini visuals in cards#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make feature cards show rather than tell.
  • Reasoning: Template bento cards contain small UI fragments, charts or states, not icons and three lines of text.
  • Constraint: Each feature card gets a small, real-looking fragment of the product (a list row, a chart, a toggle, a notification) at the top, then title and one sentence. Keep fragments monochrome with the accent only where it means something.

7. Motion detail#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Constraint: Entrance: opacity plus 8–16px rise, 500–700ms, ease-out cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.2,1), stagger 60–80ms, once. Hover: 150–200ms. No bounce, no parallax on text. Shader speed slow. Everything static under prefers-reduced-motion. See motion.

8. Craft checklist before shipping#

Check the rendered page at 1440px and 390px, light and dark where supported:

  1. One primary family; at most one partner; no faux bold or italics.
  2. Hero headline two balanced lines, no orphan, tracking tightened.
  3. Every button the same height and radius family; one primary style.
  4. All section paddings from the scale; all card paddings identical.
  5. Copy blocks within the max widths above.
  6. One radius family; borders the same alpha everywhere.
  7. One icon set, one size per context, optically centred.
  8. The hero visual is high fidelity and crisp at 2x.
  9. Accent used only for actions, links and one highlight.
  10. No text below 12px; muted text still passes contrast.
  11. Mobile hero: headline, sub and primary action visible without scrolling past a visual.
  12. Nav has five or fewer items plus one action.
  13. Nothing overflows horizontally; long words wrap.
  14. Images, logos, numbers and testimonials are real or labelled as samples.

Report which checks were inspected in a real render and which were not.

title: Starter kit
description: Load when building a landing page, marketing page or product screen without an existing design system.
html:
Load when building a landing page, marketing page or product screen without an existing design system. The kit at assets/starter.css implements the visual craft baseline as plain CSS, with presets for the style directions. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Start from the kit, then make it specific#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Reach production quality fast instead of improvising spacing, type and controls.
  • Reasoning: Written rules leave room for drift; working tokens and components do not.
  • Constraint: Copy assets/starter.css into the project (or translate its tokens into the project's Tailwind theme, CSS modules or design tokens). Wrap the page in class="g", set data-direction to the chosen direction (omit for Clean product), load the fonts that direction names, then override tokens for the brand's colours. Build the product-specific visual and copy yourself; the kit gives structure, not content.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Re-deriving a type scale and button styles by eye for each page.
    • Good: <div class="g" data-direction="warm-organic">, Fraunces and Figtree loaded, accent set to the bakery's terracotta, real photos in the hero.
  • Exceptions: Projects with a design system use theirs; borrow only patterns.

Tokens#

Token Purpose
--g-bg, --g-raised, --g-card Page, raised panels, cards
--g-fg, --g-muted Text and secondary text
--g-line, --g-border Border colour and width
--g-accent, --g-on-accent Primary action
--g-font, --g-display, --g-mono Text, display and mono families
--g-display-weight, --g-display-tracking, --g-display-case Display style
--g-btn-radius, --g-radius, --g-radius-lg Control, card and frame radii
--g-shadow, --g-btn-shadow Elevation (hard offset shadows in playful and retro)

Directions: dark-technical, luminous, editorial, warm-organic, luxury, bold, playful, brutalist, retro, trust, cinematic, commerce; default is Clean product. The preset font stacks name the families from style-directions; load them (for example with @fontsource packages or the host's font tooling) or the fallbacks render.

Components#

Layout g-wrap, g-section, g-head, g-eyebrow, g-h2; header g-header, g-logo, g-nav, g-header-links; hero g-hero, g-pill, g-display, g-lede, g-actions, g-proof, g-split, g-fullbleed; media g-frame, g-frame-art, g-window, g-window-bar, g-phone; controls g-btn with g-btn-primary, g-btn-secondary, g-btn-lg, g-btn-sm, g-input; content g-bento with g-card, g-card-visual, g-card-body and g-span-4|5|6|7, g-steps, g-metrics, g-quote, g-logos, g-marquee, g-pricing with g-plan and g-price, g-faq, g-cta, g-footer; motion g-rise with g-rise-2|3|4 (disabled under reduced motion).

Hero markup#

Pattern A, centered with product frame:

<section class="g-hero"><div class="g-wrap">
  <a class="g-pill" href="#new"><b>New</b> What changed →</a>
  <h1 class="g-display">Headline in two balanced lines.</h1>
  <p class="g-lede">One or two sentences that say what it does and for whom.</p>
  <div class="g-actions">
    <a class="g-btn g-btn-primary g-btn-lg" href="#start">Get started</a>
    <a class="g-btn g-btn-secondary g-btn-lg" href="#how">See how it works</a>
  </div>
  <div class="g-frame" style="margin-top:72px;padding:64px 64px 0">
    <div class="g-frame-art"><!-- gradient, shader or image --></div>
    <div class="g-window"><div class="g-window-bar"><i></i><i></i><i></i></div><!-- product UI --></div>
  </div>
</div></section>

Pattern B, split: put copy and visual in <div class="g-wrap g-split"> inside g-hero. Pattern C, full-bleed: <section class="g-fullbleed"> with an <img>, <video> or g-frame-art as the first child and copy in g-wrap. Pattern D, editorial: use data-direction="editorial" and let g-display run larger and left-aligned. Pattern E, waitlist: replace g-actions with a form using g-input and g-btn-primary, and put the visual in a g-frame below.

Sections#

<section class="g-section"><div class="g-wrap">
  <div class="g-head"><span class="g-eyebrow">Features</span><h2 class="g-h2">Section headline.</h2><p>One-sentence intro.</p></div>
  <div class="g-bento">
    <article class="g-card g-span-7"><div class="g-card-visual"><!-- UI fragment --></div>
      <div class="g-card-body"><h3>Card title</h3><p>One sentence.</p></div></article>
    <article class="g-card g-span-5">…</article>
  </div>
</div></section>

Pricing, FAQ, CTA and footer follow the same pattern; see class names above. Use native <details> for FAQ.

Product kit#

For apps, dashboards, admin panels and settings, load assets/product.css after starter.css. It reuses the same tokens (so direction presets still apply), adds status tokens (--g-success, --g-warning, --g-danger, --g-info, each with -subtle), density modes via data-density="compact|default|comfortable" and dark tokens via data-theme="dark". Guidance for these screens lives in product UI and forms.

Classes: shell g-app, g-sidebar (data-open on mobile), g-sidebar-label, g-nav-item (aria-current="page"), g-topbar, g-topbar-title, g-topbar-actions, g-main, g-page-head; panels g-panel, g-panel-head, g-panel-body, g-kpis, g-kpi, g-kpi-label, g-kpi-value, g-delta (data-trend="good|bad"); forms g-field, g-label, g-hint, g-error, g-select, g-textarea, g-switch, g-btn-danger, g-btn-ghost; data g-table-wrap, g-table (add data-stack and per-cell data-label to stack rows under 640px), g-num; status g-badge and g-alert (data-tone="success|warning|danger|info"), g-empty; other g-tabs, g-tab (aria-selected for real tabs, aria-pressed for filter toggles), g-kbd, g-skeleton, g-dialog (native <dialog>), g-toast.

<div class="g g-app" data-density="default">
  <nav class="g-sidebar" aria-label="Main">
    <a class="g-nav-item" href="/inbox" aria-current="page">Inbox</a>
    <span class="g-sidebar-label">Workspace</span>
    <a class="g-nav-item" href="/reports">Reports</a>
  </nav>
  <header class="g-topbar"><span class="g-topbar-title">Inbox</span>
    <div class="g-topbar-actions"><button class="g-btn g-btn-primary">New invoice</button></div></header>
  <main class="g-main">
    <div class="g-page-head"><div><h1>Needs attention</h1><p>3 invoices are overdue.</p></div></div>
    <div class="g-table-wrap"><table class="g-table">
      <thead><tr><th scope="col">Customer</th><th scope="col">Status</th><th scope="col" class="g-num">Amount</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody><tr><td>Northwind</td><td><span class="g-badge" data-tone="danger">Overdue</span></td><td class="g-num">$4,200.00</td></tr></tbody>
    </table></div>
  </main>
</div>

The mobile sidebar needs a menu button in the top bar that toggles data-open, traps focus while open and closes on Escape; the kit provides the styles, not the script.

Tailwind mapping#

Map tokens into the theme instead of hard-coding values (full approach in design tokens): colors.bg = var(--g-bg), colors.fg, colors.muted, colors.accent; borderRadius.card = var(--g-radius); fontFamily.display = var(--g-display). Keep the kit's numbers: container 1200px, section padding 120/80px, controls h-10, card padding 7, gaps 4.

After building#

Run the craft checklist in visual craft on real renders at desktop and mobile widths, in every theme the page supports.

title: Typography
description: Load when choosing typefaces, setting type hierarchy and rhythm, or loading fonts.
html:
Load when choosing typefaces, setting type hierarchy and rhythm, or loading fonts. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Choose for actual content#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Make typography fit language, brand and reading.
  • Reasoning: Category-to-personality tables oversimplify type selection.
  • Constraint: Inspect existing branding, glyph/language support, numerals, x-height, weight range, licensing and actual strings. Pair faces only when the contrast helps. A single family may be enough. Poppins is valid when considered.
  • Example:
    • Bad: All developer tools must use monospace headings.
    • Good: Compare the real product name, data table and multilingual content in candidate faces.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Set hierarchy and rhythm#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make reading and scanning comfortable.
  • Reasoning: Size, weight, spacing and line length work together.
  • Constraint: Tune measure, line-height, tracking and scale in rendered text. Roughly 45–75 characters can be a starting range for prose, not a lock. Avoid rigid tracking values or weight counts. Never claim font size alone proves accessibility.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Apply -0.04em to every script and size.
    • Good: Use the font's natural spacing for body copy, adjust large Latin headings after inspecting wraps.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Load fonts responsibly#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Preserve content while fonts load.
  • Reasoning: Missing glyphs and layout shifts affect real tasks.
  • Constraint: Use licensed fonts, fallbacks and appropriate loading strategy. Verify downloaded files are fonts, prevent synthetic weights where possible, and inspect font loading, accented text and fallback layout.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A logo-like stylistic set makes “AI” read as a star.
    • Good: Check actual glyphs and disable unsupported stylistic substitutions before changing the copy.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Color roles and contrast
description: Load when defining colour roles, palettes, contrast or light and dark themes.
html:
Load when defining colour roles, palettes, contrast or light and dark themes. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Choose roles before counts#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make color communicate coherent meaning.
  • Reasoning: A palette count cannot determine whether a screen is useful or expressive.
  • Constraint: Define background, surface, text, action, focus and semantic roles. Allow categorical colors and expressive brand palettes when their roles remain legible. Check how nearby colors compete. No universal single-accent or two-text-color lock.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Remove half the legend categories to obey a three-color rule.
    • Good: Use distinct category colors plus labels and shapes; reserve a strong action treatment for the next task.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Measure contrast in context#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep text and essential controls readable.
  • Reasoning: A hex value alone does not establish contrast over imagery or transparency.
  • Constraint: Check rendered combinations: normal text 4.5:1, large text 3:1, applicable essential UI boundaries and graphics 3:1. Use WCAG definitions of large text. Do not communicate meaning by color alone. Check focus, code, error and both themes.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A red dot alone means an overdue task.
    • Good: Show “Overdue” with an icon and measured contrast.
  • Exceptions: Inactive controls and other WCAG exceptions have specific conditions; do not extend them to readable active content.

Deliberate themes#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Retain hierarchy across modes.
  • Reasoning: Dark mode needs its own surfaces, text and semantic colors.
  • Constraint: Design each supported mode; avoid CSS inversion. Pure white or black page bases are valid when requested. Differentiate surfaces through borders, spacing, tint or elevation as appropriate. Respect the project's theme contract and persist explicit choices.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Invert all colors and assume dark charts remain readable.
    • Good: Check every semantic and code color against its actual dark surface.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Build palettes systematically#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Get predictable steps and contrast instead of guessing hex codes.
  • Reasoning: Hand-picked shades drift in lightness and saturation; perceptual spaces keep steps even.
  • Constraint: Build ramps in OKLCH and expose them through semantic tokens; see design tokens for the token set, dark-mode rules and Tailwind/shadcn mapping, and data visualization for categorical, sequential and diverging chart palettes. Tint neutrals slightly toward the brand hue. Accent usage: primary action, links, focus and one highlight; status colours only for status.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Seven blues picked by eye, two of them indistinguishable, the link blue failing 4.5:1.
    • Good: An OKLCH ramp with even lightness steps, with accent and link taken from measured steps.
  • Exceptions: A supplied brand palette; derive the missing steps around it.

title: Design tokens, theming and dark mode
description: Load when setting up or extending a design system, adding dark mode or themes, mapping a design into Tailwind/shadcn/CSS variables, or auditing hard-coded values.
html:
Load when setting up or extending a design system, adding dark mode or themes, mapping a design into Tailwind/shadcn/CSS variables, or auditing hard-coded values. Pair with color and the starter kit. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. Token architecture#

Three tiers: primitive, semantic, component#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Change the look in one place without hunting through components.
  • Reasoning: Components that reference #2563eb or blue-600 directly cannot be themed, and dark mode becomes a rewrite.
  • Constraint: Primitives hold raw values (--blue-600, --space-4). Semantic tokens name a role and point to primitives (--color-bg, --color-fg, --color-fg-muted, --color-border, --color-accent, --color-on-accent, --color-danger, --color-focus). Components use only semantic tokens, plus component tokens when a component needs its own knob (--button-radius). Themes and dark mode override semantic tokens only. Name by role, never by appearance (--color-danger, not --color-red).
  • Example:
    • Bad: .btn { background: #2563eb } repeated in twelve files, dark mode via .dark .btn { background: #3b82f6 }.
    • Good: .btn { background: var(--color-accent) }; dark mode redefines --color-accent once.
  • Exceptions: One-off marketing pages may use primitives directly if they never need theming.

The minimum semantic set#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Cover what real interfaces need without an explosion of names.
  • Reasoning: Missing roles lead to ad-hoc values; too many lead to nobody knowing which to use.
  • Constraint: Start with these and add only when a real need appears.
Group Tokens
Surfaces bg (page), surface (cards, panels), surface-raised (popovers, menus), surface-sunken (wells, code), overlay (scrim)
Text fg, fg-muted, fg-subtle (placeholder, disabled), fg-on-accent
Lines border, border-strong, focus
Action accent, accent-hover, accent-fg, accent-subtle (tinted backgrounds)
Status success, warning, danger, info, each with -fg and -subtle
Data chart-1 … chart-8 categorical; sequential and diverging ramps if charts need them
Shape radius-sm (inputs, badges), radius-md (buttons, cards), radius-lg (panels, dialogs), radius-full
Space 4px scale: 1=4, 2=8, 3=12, 4=16, 5=20, 6=24, 8=32, 10=40, 12=48, 16=64, 20=80, 24=96
Type text-xs 12, sm 14, base 16, lg 18, xl 20, 2xl 24, 3xl 30, 4xl 36, 5xl 48, 6xl 60, 7xl 72; line-heights and weights paired per step
Elevation shadow-sm (controls), shadow-md (cards on hover, dropdowns), shadow-lg (dialogs, popovers)
Motion duration-fast 120–150ms, duration-base 200–250ms, duration-slow 300–400ms; ease-out cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.2,1), ease-in-out cubic-bezier(.65,0,.35,1)
Layers z-dropdown 1000, z-sticky 1100, z-overlay 1200, z-modal 1300, z-popover 1400, z-toast 1500, z-tooltip 1600
  • Exceptions: Existing design systems keep their names; map to them instead of renaming.

2. Colour scales#

Build scales in a perceptual space#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Get evenly stepped palettes that work in both themes.
  • Reasoning: HSL lightness is not perceptual: a yellow and a blue at "50%" look wildly different, so hand-made HSL scales have uneven steps and unpredictable contrast.
  • Constraint: Define colour scales in OKLCH (oklch(L C H)), stepping lightness evenly (for example 0.98, 0.95, 0.90, 0.82, 0.72, 0.62, 0.53, 0.45, 0.37, 0.28, 0.20) and reducing chroma at the extremes. Tint neutrals slightly toward the brand hue (chroma 0.005–0.015) for warmth or coolness instead of pure grey. Provide sRGB/hex fallbacks if supporting very old browsers. Check every semantic text pair for contrast after building the scale; perceptual lightness helps but does not replace measurement.
  • Example:
    • Bad: hsl(220 90% 50%) to hsl(220 90% 90%) in 10% jumps, with the middle steps indistinguishable.
    • Good: An OKLCH blue ramp with even lightness steps, blue-600 measured at 5.2:1 on white.
  • Exceptions: A supplied brand palette; derive the missing steps around it.

3. Dark mode#

Design dark mode, do not invert it#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep hierarchy and contrast in both themes.
  • Reasoning: Inverted palettes produce glowing shadows, vibrating saturated colours and lost elevation.
  • Constraint: Dark surfaces get lighter as they rise (page darkest, cards and popovers progressively lighter), because shadows barely show on dark backgrounds; use borders at 6–12% white alpha to separate. Use near-black (#0a0a0a–#121212) or pure black if the brand wants it, and off-white text (#ededed–#fafafa) to reduce halation. Desaturate and lighten accent and status colours so they pass contrast on dark surfaces without vibrating. Re-check every chart colour, code-syntax colour, focus ring and image (logos may need a light variant; photos may need slight dimming). Set color-scheme: light dark so native controls and scrollbars match.
  • Example:
    • Bad: filter: invert(1) on the page; the brand blue becomes orange and photos turn negative.
    • Good: Separate dark tokens with an accent shifted from oklch(0.55 0.2 260) to oklch(0.72 0.15 260).
  • Exceptions: None for products that offer dark mode.

Theme switching without flash#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Respect the user's choice and avoid a flash of the wrong theme.
  • Reasoning: Reading the stored theme after hydration paints the light theme first.
  • Constraint: Default to prefers-color-scheme. Offer Light, Dark and System. Persist explicit choices (localStorage or a cookie for server rendering). Apply the theme with a tiny blocking inline script in <head> that sets data-theme or a class before first paint, wrapped in try/catch for blocked storage. Disable transitions during the switch so every element does not animate. Style both :root and [data-theme="dark"] (or .dark) from one token file.
  • Exceptions: Single-theme products.

4. Mapping tokens into common stacks#

Tailwind CSS#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Use tokens through utility classes.
  • Reasoning: Tailwind's palette classes used directly (bg-blue-600) bypass semantic roles.
  • Constraint: Tailwind v4: declare tokens in CSS with @theme { --color-bg: …; --color-accent: …; --radius-md: … } and switch themes by redefining the underlying variables under [data-theme="dark"], or use @custom-variant dark (&:where([data-theme=dark], [data-theme=dark] *));. Tailwind v3: map theme.extend.colors to var(--color-…) and set darkMode: ['selector', '[data-theme="dark"]'] (or 'class'). Components then use bg-bg, text-fg-muted, border-border, bg-accent. Check which version the project uses before writing config.
  • Exceptions: Prototypes may use the default palette, then replace it.

shadcn/ui and Radix-based kits#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Theme component libraries through their own variables.
  • Reasoning: Overriding component classes one by one fights the library's theming contract.
  • Constraint: shadcn/ui components read CSS variables such as --background, --foreground, --card, --popover, --primary, --primary-foreground, --secondary, --muted, --muted-foreground, --accent, --destructive, --border, --input, --ring, --radius and --chart-1…5. Map your semantic tokens onto those names (in :root and .dark), keep the accessible primitives untouched, and change --radius once rather than per component. Inspect the project's components.json and globals file for the exact variable names in its version.
  • Exceptions: Heavily customised component sets owned by the project.

5. Tokens checklist#

  1. No raw hex, rgb or arbitrary px values in components except deliberate one-offs.
  2. Semantic names describe roles; dark mode overrides only semantic tokens.
  3. Every text/background pair passes contrast in both themes, including status, chart and code colours.
  4. Theme applies before first paint, persists, and offers System.
  5. Spacing, radius, type, shadow, motion and z-index come from scales.

title: Icons, images and media
description: Load when choosing icons, placing photography, screenshots, logos, avatars, video or illustration, and when optimising media.
html:
Load when choosing icons, placing photography, screenshots, logos, avatars, video or illustration, and when optimising media. Pair with visual craft for the hero visual and direction / composition / assets for rights. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. Icons#

One set, one grid, one weight#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make icons read as one family.
  • Reasoning: Mixing sets (a filled Material icon next to a 1.5px Lucide outline) is an immediate sign of assembly from parts.
  • Constraint: Pick one licensed set and use it everywhere: Lucide (ISC), Phosphor (MIT), Heroicons (MIT), Tabler (MIT) or Radix Icons (MIT). Keep one stroke width (1.5px for refined, 2px for bold) and one style (outline or filled; filled may mark the active state). Sizes: 16px inline with 14px text and in dense UI, 20px in default buttons and nav, 24px for standalone or touch. Icons inherit currentColor. Optically centre icons in buttons; align to the text's cap height, not its box.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Emoji as feature icons beside outline icons, each in a different coloured circle.
    • Good: Lucide at 1.5px stroke, 16px in the table toolbar and 20px in the sidebar, all currentColor.
  • Exceptions: A brand-supplied custom icon set.

Icons support words#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep meaning clear and accessible.
  • Reasoning: Few icons are universally understood (search, close, menu, home); most need a label.
  • Constraint: Pair icons with text labels by default. Icon-only buttons are allowed for universal or repeated actions in toolbars, and must have an accessible name (aria-label or visually hidden text) plus a tooltip on hover and focus. Decorative icons next to a text label get aria-hidden="true". Do not use an icon per feature card just to fill space; use a product fragment instead (see visual craft).
  • Exceptions: None for accessible names.

2. Images and photography#

Choose real, relevant images#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Show something true about the product.
  • Reasoning: Generic stock (handshakes, people pointing at laptops) and unrelated scenery signal filler.
  • Constraint: Prefer, in order: real product screenshots or UI built in code, the client's own photography, licensed photography that depicts the actual subject, then generated or abstract visuals clearly not pretending to be real people or results. Record the source and licence. Never use images of real people as fake customers or team members.
  • Exceptions: Explicit mood boards and concept work, labelled as such.

Art-direct and frame consistently#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make a set of images look like one product.
  • Reasoning: Mixed aspect ratios, colour temperatures and crops make a page feel collaged.
  • Constraint: Pick a small set of aspect ratios (16:9 or 3:2 for media, 4:5 for portraits and product cards, 1:1 for avatars and thumbnails) and use aspect-ratio with object-fit: cover; set object-position to keep the subject. Keep colour treatment consistent (same temperature, similar contrast; a subtle overlay can unify). Screenshots sit in a frame (border, radius 12–24px, soft shadow) at 2x resolution, cropped to the relevant part rather than the whole screen. Text over images needs a scrim or gradient and a measured contrast check at every breakpoint.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A 4:3 team photo, a 16:9 office photo and a square logo in one row, each a different height.
    • Good: Three 4:5 portraits, same crop height, same warm grade.
  • Exceptions: Editorial layouts that deliberately vary scale.

Alt text that does a job#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Convey the image's purpose to people who cannot see it.
  • Reasoning: "image.png" and "photo" are noise; a full description of a decorative image is also noise.
  • Constraint: Informative images: describe what matters in context in one sentence, without "image of". Images that are links or buttons: describe the destination or action. Decorative images: alt="". Charts and diagrams: short alt plus a text or table alternative nearby. Text in images: include the text in the alt (and avoid text in images).
  • Exceptions: None.

3. Logos, avatars and brand marks#

Handle logos with care#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Present marks accurately and legally.
  • Reasoning: Squashed, recoloured or invented "customer" logos damage trust and may infringe.
  • Constraint: Use only logos you have permission to show and that represent real relationships. Use SVG; never stretch; keep clear space; provide light and dark variants or a monochrome version for logo walls. Size logo walls by optical weight, not equal width. Avatars: circle or rounded square, initials fallback on a tinted background derived from the name, consistent sizes (24/32/40/64px).
  • Exceptions: Clearly labelled fictional brands in demos.

4. Delivering media#

Fast, stable, sharp#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep pages fast and free of layout shift.
  • Reasoning: Unsized and oversized images are the most common cause of slow loading and jumping layouts.
  • Constraint: Always set width and height (or aspect-ratio) so space is reserved. Serve AVIF or WebP with responsive srcset/sizes (or the framework's image component, such as next/image). Lazy-load images below the fold (loading="lazy") but never the LCP hero image; give the hero fetchpriority="high" and preload it if it is a CSS background. Export UI screenshots at 2x and compress. Use SVG for icons, logos and simple illustrations, and strip editor metadata. Video: muted, playsinline, a poster image, no autoplay with sound, controls available, and a reduced-motion alternative for background video.
  • Exceptions: None.

5. Media checklist#

  1. One icon set, one stroke and style, sizes from 16/20/24.
  2. Icon-only controls have accessible names and tooltips.
  3. Images are real or clearly illustrative, sourced and licensed.
  4. Consistent aspect ratios and colour treatment; text over images passes contrast.
  5. Alt text matches purpose; decorative images use alt="".
  6. Every image reserves space; hero is prioritised; others lazy-load; formats are modern.

title: Backgrounds and surfaces
description: Load when choosing page surfaces, background imagery, gradients or textures.
html:
Load when choosing page surfaces, background imagery, gradients or textures. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Choose from the content#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Support readability and relevant personality.
  • Reasoning: Category-based background recipes can become another skin.
  • Constraint: Select white, black, tinted, photographic, illustrated or textured surfaces according to brand, content and task. Do not force warm paper, charcoal or a fixed palette on every product. A requested pure-white or pure-black base is valid.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Every developer product must be dark and monospaced.
    • Good: Follow the established identity and inspect text, focus and semantics on actual surfaces.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Layer without obscuring#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make surfaces distinguishable where needed.
  • Reasoning: Tint, borders, spacing and elevation can all establish hierarchy.
  • Constraint: Choose the minimum surface differentiation that makes roles clear. Gradients, patterns, noise and glass are optional. Check text over all image/scroll states. Avoid global blur or fixed opacity recipes as substitutes for measured contrast.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A translucent header disappears over a changing photo.
    • Good: Use a sufficiently opaque header surface and verify the scrolled state.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Product UI: apps, dashboards and tools
description: Load for any logged-in product surface: web apps, dashboards, admin panels, internal tools, settings, editors, developer tools and data-heavy screens.
html:
Load for any logged-in product surface: web apps, dashboards, admin panels, internal tools, settings, editors, developer tools and data-heavy screens. Landing pages use visual craft and landing composition instead; ready-made product components live in assets/product.css (see the starter kit). Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Product UI is used daily, for hours, by people trying to finish work. Optimise for speed of recognition, density that matches the task, predictable placement and recoverable actions. Expressiveness belongs in onboarding, empty states and moments of success, not in every panel.

1. Start from the job#

Name the primary loop#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make the screen serve the work it exists for.
  • Reasoning: Most product screens fail by showing everything at equal weight; users then hunt for the one thing they came to do.
  • Constraint: Before layout, write one sentence: "A [role] opens this to [verb] [object] and leaves when [done condition]." Lead the screen with the object of that verb (the queue, the document, the failing check), and keep the primary action within one click of it. Secondary information goes to a side panel, a tab or a details view.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A dispatcher dashboard opens on four KPI tiles, a revenue chart and a welcome banner; late deliveries are three scrolls down.
    • Good: The same dashboard opens on "4 deliveries need attention", sorted by lateness, with Reassign inline; KPIs sit in a compact strip above.
  • Exceptions: Executive reporting screens whose job really is the overview.

Choose a density mode#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Match spacing to how often and how long people use the screen.
  • Reasoning: Marketing spacing (120px sections, 48px buttons) wastes the screen in a daily tool; cramped density tires occasional users.
  • Constraint: Pick one mode per surface and apply it consistently.
Mode Use for Body / label Control height Table row Panel padding Gaps
Comfortable Consumer apps, onboarding, settings, occasional use 15–16px / 14px 40px 52–56px 24px 16–24px
Default Most SaaS and admin 14px / 13–14px 36px 44–48px 16–20px 12–16px
Compact Ops consoles, trading, logs, spreadsheets, IDE-like tools 13px / 12–13px 28–32px 32–36px 12px 8px
  • Example:
    • Bad: A log viewer with 56px rows showing nine lines per screen.
    • Good: The log viewer at 32px rows in a monospace column, with a density toggle for people who want more air.
  • Exceptions: Touch-first products keep 44px targets regardless of mode.

2. The app shell#

Shell anatomy#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Give every screen the same predictable frame.
  • Reasoning: People navigate by position. A shell that shifts between pages forces them to re-read it.
  • Constraint: Sidebar 240–280px expanded (56–64px collapsed, icons with tooltips and accessible names), top bar 48–56px with page title, breadcrumbs when hierarchy is deeper than two levels, and page actions on the right. Content area scrolls independently; the shell does not. Keep the primary navigation to 5–9 top-level destinations, grouped with small muted section labels. Put account, workspace switcher and settings at the sidebar's top or bottom, never mixed into feature navigation. Mark the current destination with background tint plus weight or an indicator, and aria-current="page".
  • Example:
    • Bad: 22 flat sidebar links, the current page shown only by a colour change, page actions floating in different spots per screen.
    • Good: Six grouped destinations, a tinted current row, title and actions in a consistent top bar.
  • Exceptions: Single-purpose tools (an editor, a canvas) may hide the shell to maximise the work area, with a clear way back.

Mobile shell#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep every destination reachable on small screens.
  • Reasoning: A squeezed desktop sidebar either covers content or disappears.
  • Constraint: Below about 768px, move navigation into a drawer opened from the top bar (focus trapped, Escape closes, focus returns to the trigger), or a bottom tab bar of at most five destinations for consumer apps. Tables become stacked cards or keep a scoped horizontal scroll with the key column sticky. Page actions collapse into one primary button plus an overflow menu.
  • Exceptions: Desktop-only internal tools may state their supported widths, but must still not break at zoom.

3. Common screens#

Dashboards#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
