  • Purpose: Turn numbers into a decision.
  • Reasoning: Dashboards default to a wall of equal tiles; nobody knows which number matters.
  • Constraint: Order by decision: exceptions and alerts first, then the few metrics that indicate health, then trends, then reference detail. Each KPI shows value, unit, comparison period and direction with text (not colour alone), for example "↑ 12% vs last week". Use a sparkline only when the shape matters. Two to five KPIs is typical; no fixed count. Every chart answers a question written as its title ("Signups are flat since the pricing change"), or a neutral label when the reader must judge. Link each tile to the list behind it. Read data visualization for charts.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Eight identical tiles with icons in coloured circles and no comparison.
    • Good: "3 invoices overdue" with a Review action, then MRR, churn and active seats with week-over-week deltas.
  • Exceptions: Wallboards viewed from a distance use larger type and fewer items.

Lists and tables#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make records scannable, comparable and actionable.
  • Reasoning: Tables are where product users spend most of their time; small inconsistencies multiply across hundreds of rows.
  • Constraint: Use a real <table> with <th scope="col"> for tabular data. Left-align text, right-align numbers and use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; align headers with their column content. Keep the identifying column first and sticky when scrolling horizontally; make the header sticky when scrolling vertically. Show sort state with an icon and aria-sort. Row hover is a subtle tint; selected rows use a stronger tint plus a checkbox. Bulk actions appear in a bar when rows are selected, stating the count. Truncate long text with an ellipsis and a full-value tooltip or title only when the full value is also reachable elsewhere. Provide loading (skeleton rows at real row height), empty (explain and offer the next action) and error (what failed, Retry) states. Paginate or virtualise beyond a few hundred rows; state the range ("1–50 of 1,284").
  • Example:
    • Bad: Centered columns, proportional digits that jitter, a spinner replacing the whole table on every sort.
    • Good: Right-aligned tabular amounts, sticky customer column, rows dimmed during refetch while keeping their position.
  • Exceptions: Card lists suit visual objects (files with previews, products, people with photos).

Detail views and side panels#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Inspect or edit one record without losing the list.
  • Reasoning: Full-page navigation for every record breaks flow in triage work.
  • Constraint: Use a right side panel (400–560px) for quick inspect/edit from a list, a full page for complex records with their own sub-navigation. Panels have a title, a close button, keyboard Escape, and keep the URL addressable when the record should be shareable. Put the record's status and primary action at the top; metadata in a two-column label/value list; activity history at the bottom.
  • Exceptions: Mobile always uses a full screen.

Settings#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make configuration safe and findable.
  • Reasoning: Settings accumulate; without structure they become a junk drawer.
  • Constraint: Group by object (Profile, Workspace, Billing, Notifications, Security, Integrations) in a secondary nav. Each setting is label, one-line description of the consequence, then control. Choose one save model per page: instant save with a small "Saved" confirmation for toggles, or an explicit Save bar that appears when the form is dirty and warns on navigation away. Put destructive actions in a separated "Danger zone" with a confirmation that names the object (type the project name for irreversible deletes).
  • Exceptions: Very small settings surfaces can be a single page.

Onboarding and empty states#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Turn the first blank screen into the first success.
  • Reasoning: An empty product looks broken; a wizard that blocks exploration feels like a toll gate.
  • Constraint: Empty states say what will appear here, why it is empty, and offer the one action that fills it (plus import or sample data where useful). Distinguish first-use empty, no-results-for-filter (offer Clear filters) and error-empty. Prefer progressive checklists over blocking multi-step tours; let people skip. Illustrations are optional and should be small.
  • Exceptions: Regulated setup (KYC, payments) that must complete before use.

Command palette and shortcuts#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Give frequent users speed without hiding features from new ones.
  • Reasoning: Power users live on the keyboard; shortcuts nobody can discover are dead weight.
  • Constraint: Cmd/Ctrl+K opens a palette that searches navigation, records and actions, with arrow keys, Enter, Escape and a visible shortcut hint per item. Show shortcuts in tooltips and menus with <kbd>. Never override browser or screen-reader shortcuts; single-key shortcuts must be disableable or only active when a component has focus (WCAG 2.1.4). Provide a "?" shortcut sheet in keyboard-heavy tools.
  • Exceptions: Simple consumer apps may not need a palette.

4. Feedback and system status#

Make every action answer#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Let people trust what the system did.
  • Reasoning: Silent saves and spinners without end are the main source of "did that work?" anxiety.
  • Constraint: Respond within 100ms (pressed state, optimistic change or inline spinner). Over about 1s show progress in place; over about 10s allow leaving and notify on completion. Use inline confirmation near the control for small actions, a toast (4–6s, pausable, not the only record of errors) for background completion, and a banner for persistent conditions (offline, trial ending, degraded service). Offer Undo for reversible destructive actions instead of a confirm dialog. Use role="status" or aria-live="polite" for non-urgent announcements and role="alert" only for urgent errors.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "Are you sure?" before archiving an email, then nothing visible happens.
    • Good: The email archives instantly with "Archived · Undo" for six seconds.
  • Exceptions: Irreversible or costly actions (payments, deletion of shared data) need explicit confirmation.

Status, badges and permissions#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Communicate state without noise.
  • Reasoning: When every row has three coloured pills, none of them stands out.
  • Constraint: Badges are small (20–24px high, 12px text), use a tinted background with a readable text colour, and always include a word. Reserve saturated colour for states that need action. Show disabled controls with a reason (tooltip or helper text) when a permission or plan limit blocks them, or hide controls the user can never use.
  • Exceptions: Dense monitoring views may use a dot plus label.

5. Product craft checklist#

Inspect real renders at 1440px, 1024px and 390px, light and dark where supported:

  1. The primary loop is visible without scrolling and its action is one click away.
  2. One density mode applied consistently; control heights match across buttons, inputs and selects.
  3. Shell does not shift between pages; current location is marked and announced.
  4. Numbers are right-aligned and tabular; units and comparison periods are present.
  5. Every list has loading, empty, no-results and error states with geometry that does not jump.
  6. Every action gives feedback within 100ms; long work shows progress; errors say how to recover.
  7. Destructive actions offer Undo or a confirmation naming the object.
  8. Keyboard: tab order follows layout, focus is visible, Escape closes overlays, palette and shortcuts work.
  9. Disabled controls explain why.
  10. Mobile: navigation reachable, tables readable, primary action reachable by thumb.

Report which checks were inspected in a real render and which were not.

title: Forms, input and validation
description: Load for sign-up, checkout, settings, onboarding, search, filters, multi-step flows and any screen where people type or choose.
html:
Load for sign-up, checkout, settings, onboarding, search, filters, multi-step flows and any screen where people type or choose. Pair with UX writing for labels and error text and accessibility. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. Fields#

Every field has a persistent label#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep the question visible while answering it.
  • Reasoning: Placeholder-only fields lose their label on the first keystroke, fail screen readers and look filled-in when empty.
  • Constraint: A visible <label for> above the field (top-aligned labels scan fastest). Help text sits between label and field or below it, linked with aria-describedby. Placeholders show an example format only ("name@company.com"), never the label or instructions. Mark the minority: if most fields are required, mark optional ones "(optional)"; otherwise mark required ones, and set required/aria-required.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A grey "Email" placeholder that vanishes, asterisks with no legend.
    • Good: Label "Work email", hint "We'll send the invite here", placeholder "you@company.com".
  • Exceptions: A single search field with a visible search button and an accessible name may omit the visible label.

Use the right input#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Get the right keyboard, autofill and validation for free.
  • Reasoning: Browsers and password managers already solve most input problems when given the correct attributes.
  • Constraint: Set type (email, tel, url, number only for quantities, password, search, date where the native picker suits the audience), inputmode (numeric for codes and card numbers, decimal for amounts), and autocomplete tokens (name, email, street-address, postal-code, cc-number, one-time-code, new-password, current-password). Never block paste. Use spellcheck="false" and autocapitalize="off" for usernames, codes and emails.
  • Example:
    • Bad: type="number" for a card number, which strips leading zeros and shows spinners.
    • Good: type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="cc-number".
  • Exceptions: None for autocomplete on personal data fields.

Choose controls by number of options#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Minimise effort per choice.
  • Reasoning: A dropdown hides two options behind an extra click; radio buttons for forty countries are unreadable.
  • Constraint: 2 options: switch (immediate effect) or radio/segmented control (submitted with the form). 3–6: radio group or segmented control, all visible. 7–15: select. More than 15 or searchable data: combobox with type-ahead. Multiple choice: checkboxes (few) or multi-select combobox with chips (many). Dates: three fields or a text field for known dates (birthdays), a calendar picker for nearby dates (bookings). Size fields to the expected input (postcode short, address long).
  • Exceptions: Brand or space constraints may justify a select for 4–6 options on mobile.

2. Validation#

Validate at the right moment#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Catch errors early without nagging.
  • Reasoning: Errors on every keystroke punish people mid-typing; errors only after submit send them hunting.
  • Constraint: Validate a field on blur once it has been touched, then live on input while it is invalid so the error clears as soon as it is fixed. Validate everything on submit. Never disable the submit button to signal invalid input; let people submit and show what is wrong. Show server errors (taken username, declined card) next to the relevant field. Keep entered values after any error, including server errors and page reloads where possible.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "Invalid email" appears after typing "j", and the greyed-out Submit gives no reason.
    • Good: On blur, "Enter an email address like name@example.com"; it disappears the moment the address becomes valid.
  • Exceptions: Password strength meters and character counters may update live from the first keystroke.

Write errors that fix themselves#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Tell people exactly how to recover.
  • Reasoning: "Invalid input" is a judgment, not an instruction.
  • Constraint: Error text says what to do, in plain words, next to the field, in the danger colour with an icon (never colour alone), linked with aria-describedby and aria-invalid="true". On submit with errors, move focus to the first invalid field, or to an error summary at the top for long forms, listing each error as a link to its field. Accept flexible formats (spaces in phone and card numbers, any case in emails) and normalise them yourself rather than rejecting them.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "Error: field 3 format invalid".
    • Good: "Enter the date as DD/MM/YYYY, for example 07/03/1990".
  • Exceptions: Security-sensitive errors (login) stay generic: "Email or password is incorrect".

3. Structure and flow#

Fewer fields, logical groups#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Reduce abandonment.
  • Reasoning: Each field costs attention; unexplained fields cost trust.
  • Constraint: Remove every field you cannot justify; ask later for anything not needed now. One column for most forms (multi-column only for tightly related short fields such as city/postcode or first/last name). Group related fields with <fieldset> and <legend>. Order fields the way people think (name before address before payment). Explain why you ask for sensitive data next to the field.
  • Exceptions: Dense internal admin forms may use two columns at wide widths.

Multi-step flows#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make long processes feel finite and safe.
  • Reasoning: People abandon flows when they cannot see the end or fear losing work.
  • Constraint: Split by topic, not by an arbitrary field count. Show progress as named steps ("Account · Workspace · Invite"), not only a percentage. Allow Back without losing data, save drafts automatically for long flows, and show a review step before irreversible submission. The primary button names the next step ("Continue to payment"), the last one names the outcome ("Pay $48").
  • Exceptions: Two or three short questions fit on one page.

Buttons and submission#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Prevent double submits and ambiguity.
  • Reasoning: Slow networks turn impatient clicks into duplicate orders.
  • Constraint: One primary button per form, labelled with the specific action ("Create project", not "Submit"). While submitting, keep the label width stable, show an inline spinner, set aria-busy and ignore further clicks; re-enable on failure. Enter submits single-line forms. Cancel is a secondary or text button, placed consistently. Confirm success with the result, not just a toast ("Project created" and the project open).
  • Exceptions: Instant-save settings have no submit button.

4. Special inputs#

Input Do
Password Show/hide toggle with an accessible name; show requirements up front and tick them live; allow paste and password managers; autocomplete="new-password" on sign-up.
One-time code One field (autocomplete="one-time-code", inputmode="numeric"), or segmented boxes that accept paste of the full code and move focus automatically; offer resend with a countdown.
Search type="search", a clear button, results that update after a short debounce (150–300ms) or on Enter, and a "No results for 'x'" state with suggestions.
File upload A real button plus drop zone; state accepted types and size limit before upload; show per-file progress, errors and remove; keep the file list after validation errors.
Money Currency symbol as a prefix outside the editable text, inputmode="decimal", format on blur, store minor units.
Phone One field accepting any formatting, with a country selector defaulting from locale.
Address Autocomplete where available, always with a manual entry fallback; country first because it changes the remaining fields.
Toggles A switch means immediate effect; label states what is on ("Email me weekly reports"), not "Enable".

5. Forms checklist#

  1. Every field has a visible label, correct type, inputmode and autocomplete.
  2. Required/optional marked consistently; hints linked with aria-describedby.
  3. Errors appear on blur/submit, explain the fix, use icon plus text, and focus moves to the first error.
  4. Values survive errors; submit is never disabled to signal invalidity; double-submit is prevented.
  5. Keyboard only: tab order matches visual order, Enter submits, custom controls work with arrows and Space.
  6. Zoom to 200% and 320px width: labels, errors and buttons still visible without horizontal scroll.
  7. Success state confirms the actual result.

title: Data visualization
description: Load for charts, KPI tiles, sparklines, maps, reports and any screen that turns numbers into a judgment.
sections: 1. Choose the form from the question
html:
Load for charts, KPI tiles, sparklines, maps, reports and any screen that turns numbers into a judgment. Pair with product UI for dashboards and color for palettes. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. Choose the form from the question#

Start with the question, not the chart type#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make every chart answer something.
  • Reasoning: Charts picked for variety ("let's add a donut") decorate instead of inform.
  • Constraint: Write the question the reader brings, then pick the simplest form that answers it.
Question Use Avoid
How is one number doing? Big number + delta + comparison period; sparkline if shape matters Gauge, single-value donut
How does it change over time? Line (continuous), column (discrete periods, under ~20 bars) Area stacks with many series, 3D
How do categories compare? Horizontal bar, sorted by value, labels on the left Pie with more than 3 slices, radar
What is the share of a whole? Stacked bar or 100% bar; a pie/donut only for 2–3 parts Many-slice pie
How is it distributed? Histogram, box/strip plot Bar of averages hiding spread
How do two measures relate? Scatter, optionally sized Dual-axis line
Where is it happening? Choropleth with normalised values, or a bar chart of regions Raw counts on a map (it just shows population)
How does a flow progress? Funnel as horizontal bars with step conversion Sankey for a simple funnel
What exactly is the value? A table Any chart
  • Example:
    • Bad: A seven-slice donut of revenue by plan, colours hard to tell apart.
    • Good: A sorted horizontal bar of revenue by plan with values at the bar ends.
  • Exceptions: Brand storytelling pages may use bespoke visuals if the reading stays accurate.

Tell the reader what to see#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Lower the effort to reach the insight.
  • Reasoning: A neutral title forces every reader to do the analysis again.
  • Constraint: In reports and narrative dashboards, title with the takeaway ("Churn halved after onboarding redesign") and put the metric name and unit in the subtitle. Annotate the event that explains a change directly on the chart. In exploratory tools where readers form their own judgment, use neutral descriptive titles.
  • Exceptions: Monitoring views use neutral labels.

2. Encoding and honesty#

Keep scales truthful#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Avoid misleading readers.
  • Reasoning: Truncated baselines and inconsistent scales exaggerate change.
  • Constraint: Bar and area charts start at zero. Line charts may zoom the y-axis but must label it clearly. Small multiples share the same scale unless labelled otherwise. Do not use dual y-axes; use two aligned charts. Use the same period for comparisons and say which ("vs previous 7 days"). Label estimates, forecasts and incomplete periods (dashed line, lighter fill, "partial" label for the current week).
  • Exceptions: Log scales for data spanning orders of magnitude, clearly labelled.

Reduce ink, keep the data#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Let the data be the loudest element.
  • Reasoning: Heavy grids, borders and legends compete with the marks.
  • Constraint: Light horizontal gridlines only (border colour at low alpha), no vertical grid for time series, no chart borders or background fills, no 3D, no drop shadows. Axis text 11–12px muted; 4–6 ticks with round values. Label lines directly at their end instead of a legend when there are 2–5 series. Lines 1.5–2px; bars with 2–4px radius at the end only, gaps about 30–50% of bar width.
  • Exceptions: Print and presentation charts may need heavier weights.

3. Colour for data#

Use palettes by data type#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Map colour to meaning.
  • Reasoning: Rainbow scales and brand-coloured categories make data harder to read and harder for colour-blind readers.
  • Constraint: Categorical: up to 6–8 distinct hues of similar lightness, ordered so adjacent series differ most; beyond eight, group into "Other" or use small multiples. Sequential (low→high): one hue varying lightness, light = low on light themes. Diverging (below/above a midpoint): two hues with a neutral middle, midpoint meaningful (zero, target, average). Highlight: grey everything, colour the one series the story is about. Never encode with red/green alone; add labels, position or shape. Check the palette with a colour-vision-deficiency simulator and against both theme backgrounds (3:1 for marks that carry meaning).
  • Example:
    • Bad: A rainbow heatmap where yellow, the brightest colour, sits in the middle of the range.
    • Good: A single-blue sequential scale with a labelled legend from 0 to 1,000.
  • Exceptions: Established domain conventions (election maps, terrain) when they are understood by the audience.

Status colours carry meaning only#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep semantic colours trustworthy.
  • Reasoning: If brand green and "healthy" green are the same, every green chart looks like good news.
  • Constraint: Reserve success, warning and danger hues for status. Do not use them as categorical series. Define which direction is good per metric (lower churn is good) so a falling line is not automatically red.
  • Exceptions: None.

4. Numbers and labels#

Format numbers for humans#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make values readable and comparable.
  • Reasoning: "1234567.891" in a tile is noise; inconsistent decimals look like errors.
  • Constraint: Use Intl.NumberFormat with the user's locale. Abbreviate large numbers in tiles and axes (1.2M, 34.5K) but show the full value in tooltips and tables. Same decimal places within a column or series. Percentages: 0 decimals for big shares, 1 for small changes. Always show units and currency. Deltas carry a sign and an arrow plus words ("+12%", "↓ 3 pts"). Use tabular-nums wherever numbers update or align. Dates: relative for recent events ("5 min ago") with the absolute time on hover/focus; absolute and unambiguous elsewhere ("12 Mar 2026").
  • Exceptions: Scientific and financial contexts may require exact precision everywhere.

5. Interaction and access#

Tooltips, states and alternatives#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make exact values available to everyone.
  • Reasoning: Hover-only tooltips exclude keyboard, touch and screen-reader users.
  • Constraint: Tooltips follow the nearest point on the x-axis (crosshair) rather than requiring a precise hover; show all series values at that x, sorted, with series colour keys. Make the chart focusable with arrow-key navigation, or provide the data as a table (visible toggle or visually hidden). Give the chart an accessible name and a short text summary of the takeaway. Loading: a skeleton at final size. Empty: say there is no data for the period and suggest a wider range. Error: explain and retry. Keep chart geometry stable while data loads.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A canvas chart with no text alternative and tooltips only on hover over 4px dots.
    • Good: A crosshair tooltip, "View as table" toggle and aria-label="Weekly signups, up 18% over 8 weeks".
  • Exceptions: Decorative sparklines inside a tile that already states the value can be aria-hidden.

Responsive charts#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Keep charts legible on small screens.
  • Reasoning: Shrinking a desktop chart makes labels collide.
  • Constraint: Reduce ticks and series on narrow widths, rotate to horizontal bars instead of tilting labels, move direct labels or legends below the chart, and let detailed charts link to a full-screen view. Minimum chart height about 200px on mobile.
  • Exceptions: None.

6. Data visualization checklist#

  1. The chart type matches the question; a table would not be clearer.
  2. Title states the takeaway or the neutral metric; units and period are visible.
  3. Bars start at zero; comparisons share periods and scales; partial data is marked.
  4. Palette matches the data type, survives colour-vision simulation and both themes.
  5. Numbers are localised, abbreviated consistently and tabular.
  6. Exact values are reachable without hover; the chart has an accessible name and summary.
  7. Loading, empty and error states keep the chart's size.

title: Components and interaction states
description: Load when designing or reviewing individual components and their interaction states.
sections: State behavior is part of design
html:
Load when designing or reviewing individual components and their interaction states. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Choose structure from the task#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make components support the screen hierarchy.
  • Reasoning: An identical card anatomy or KPI row cannot fit every interface.
  • Constraint: Use the component patterns below when relevant, preserving semantics and coherent roles. Do not force exactly four KPIs, three plans, card icons, or a review carousel. Keep requirements separate from optional patterns.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Every screen starts with the same cards and footer.
    • Good: An operations screen leads with exceptions; a reading tool leads with navigable text.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

State behavior is part of design#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make controls trustworthy and recoverable.
  • Reasoning: The ideal screenshot hides loading, failure and interruption.
  • Constraint: Provide appropriate names, keyboard behavior, visible focus, loading/empty/error/success/disabled states and truthful outcomes. Keep hover optional and available actions reachable on touch.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A clickable card has no keyboard action or visible focus.
    • Good: Use a real link for navigation and a named button for an action.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Focused patterns (adapt to actual content)#

Component Useful starting point and behavior
Navigation Clear identity, current location and reachable primary destinations. Sticky behavior is optional; protect anchor and focus visibility.
Forms Persistent labels, associated descriptions/errors, understandable required/optional status; choose grouping from task complexity.
Authentication Keep the entry task clear and recovery available; respect the real provider and existing security flow. No invented working authentication.
Settings Group related choices, explain consequences and report real save status. Sidebar or sections depend on scale.
Dashboards Prioritize the decision or next action. Use metrics and charts only when relevant; no fixed KPI count.
Tables Real headers, meaningful alignment, sort state, empty/error/loading behavior; choose wrapping or scoped scrolling by content.
Pricing Make billing period, limits and total price clear. Highlight a recommendation only when justified; never invent popularity.
Cards Group related content only when a boundary helps; varied anatomy can serve varied roles.
Search Implement real matching with loading/empty/error feedback where needed. A decorative search box is not a feature.
Command palette Make shortcuts truthful; support keyboard movement, activation, Escape and managed focus.
Modals/dialogs Use accessible primitives where available; label, contain focus appropriately and return focus after closing.
Empty states Explain the absence and a relevant next action; an illustration is optional.
Loading Keep useful content and stable geometry; choose skeleton, inline progress or another appropriate signal.
Errors/alerts Explain what failed and how to recover; text/icon meaning accompanies semantic color.
Success Confirm actual completion and a useful next step when needed; avoid duplicate announcements.
Pagination Indicate current range/page and unavailable directions; endless loading is a separate choice, not a default.
Filters Show current selection and a way to clear it; preserve context and communicate result changes.
Charts/graphs Labels, units, axes, legend and exact-value access where appropriate. Allow meaningful categorical colors; offer non-hover access.
Documentation Readable measure, section navigation and accurate anchors. Three columns can help large docs; simpler structures can fit shorter guides.
Developer tools/code Monospace code, real commands, readable overflow and working copy feedback; syntax colors must remain legible.
Layered/glass panels Only use when layering serves the composition; measure text against actual backdrop states.
Reviews Use real attributed testimonials only; choose a readable list, carousel or other layout from content. No invented ratings/outcomes.
Product/quantity selectors Clear selected state, availability, price impact and keyboard/touch behavior. Reflect actual business rules.
Tooltips/data inspection Provide essential information outside hover; handle delays, focus and adjacent tooltip transitions coherently.

title: UX writing and content
description: Load whenever the interface has words: headlines, buttons, labels, errors, empty states, notifications, onboarding, pricing and confirmation dialogs.
html:
Load whenever the interface has words: headlines, buttons, labels, errors, empty states, notifications, onboarding, pricing and confirmation dialogs. Interface copy is design material; write it before polishing the layout. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. Real words first#

Never design with placeholder text#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make layout decisions with the content that will ship.
  • Reasoning: Lorem ipsum hides long names, awkward wraps and missing information; "Feature one" hides that the feature has no clear benefit.
  • Constraint: Write real, specific copy for the product before composing. Use realistic sample data with real lengths (long names, large numbers, empty values, non-English names). Label fictional data as sample data when it could be mistaken for real results. Never invent testimonials, customer logos, metrics or awards.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet" under "Feature 1".
    • Good: "Reconcile 2,000 transactions in the time it takes to make coffee", written from a real capability.
  • Exceptions: Wireframes explicitly marked as structure-only.

Be specific, not grand#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Earn trust with concrete claims.
  • Reasoning: Generic superlatives are the clearest sign of unconsidered, machine-written copy.
  • Constraint: Say what the product does, for whom, and the result. Replace adjectives with facts, numbers or examples. Avoid stock phrases: "unlock the power of", "revolutionize", "seamless", "cutting-edge", "next-generation", "supercharge", "elevate", "in today's fast-paced world", "take X to the next level", "all-in-one solution". Avoid em-dash-heavy rhythm, triplet lists in every sentence and rhetorical questions as headlines.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "Unlock the power of seamless, AI-driven collaboration."
    • Good: "Meeting notes that write themselves, with action items assigned before the call ends."
  • Exceptions: An established brand voice that uses a specific register.

2. Interface text#

Labels and buttons#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make every action predictable.
  • Reasoning: People read buttons, not paragraphs; vague verbs cause hesitation.
  • Constraint: Buttons start with a verb and name the object or outcome: "Create invoice", "Send 3 invites", "Pay $48". Avoid "OK", "Submit", "Yes/No", "Click here". Keep the same verb across the flow (the "Delete" button in the dialog that opened from "Delete"). Sentence case for labels, buttons, headings and menu items. Links describe the destination ("Read the pricing FAQ"), never "here". Two to four words for buttons, one to three for nav items.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Dialog "Are you sure?" with "Yes" / "No".
    • Good: "Delete 'Q3 report'? This removes it for everyone in Marketing." with "Delete report" / "Cancel".
  • Exceptions: Universally understood short actions (Save, Cancel, Close, Next).

Errors, warnings and empty states#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Help people recover.
  • Reasoning: An error message that blames or confuses turns a small problem into abandonment.
  • Constraint: Errors: what happened, why if known, and what to do next, without blame, jargon or error codes in the main text ("We couldn't save your changes because you're offline. They're kept here and will save when you reconnect."). Put codes in a secondary detail for support. Empty states: what will appear, why it is empty, the action to fill it. Warnings: the consequence before the action, not after. Never use humour in errors involving money, data loss or security.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "Error 500. Something went wrong."
    • Good: "We couldn't load your invoices. Check your connection and try again." [Try again]
  • Exceptions: None.

Notifications and confirmations#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Inform without interrupting.
  • Reasoning: Every toast competes for attention; vague success messages add nothing.
  • Constraint: Confirm the specific result ("Invoice INV-204 sent to Dana"), offer the next or undo action when useful, and keep it to one line. Do not announce the obvious (a toggle that visibly toggled). Notification emails and push messages start with the information, not the brand.
  • Exceptions: Celebratory moments for genuine milestones.

3. Voice, tone and format#

Consistent voice, adaptive tone#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Make the product sound like one author.
  • Reasoning: Mixed "you/your" and "I/my", formal and slangy, makes a product feel assembled.
  • Constraint: Define voice in three adjectives with what each does not mean (for example "direct, not curt"). Address the user as "you"; refer to the product as "we" sparingly. Tone shifts with context: calm and precise for errors and money, warmer for onboarding and success. Use the user's vocabulary from support tickets and interviews, not internal jargon or feature codenames.
  • Exceptions: Brands with a defined voice guide.

Format for scanning#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Let people get the point in seconds.
  • Reasoning: People scan interface text in an F-pattern; they read the first words of each line.
  • Constraint: Front-load the key words. One idea per sentence; sentences under about 20 words in UI text. Numerals for numbers ("3 seats", not "three seats"). Consistent formats for dates, times, currency and units, localised with Intl. Use the Oxford comma or not, but consistently. Avoid ALL CAPS for anything longer than a short label.
  • Exceptions: Long-form editorial content.

4. Internationalisation-ready copy#

Write and build for other languages#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep the interface usable when translated or used in other locales.
  • Reasoning: German and Finnish strings run 30–40% longer; Arabic and Hebrew run right to left; concatenated strings cannot be translated correctly.
  • Constraint: Never build sentences by concatenating fragments; use full strings with placeholders and plural rules (ICU MessageFormat or Intl.PluralRules). Leave room for 30–40% text expansion in buttons and nav. Use CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline, inset-inline-end) and dir="auto"/dir="rtl" support so layouts mirror. Do not put text in images. Format dates, numbers, currency and lists with Intl. Set lang on the document and on foreign-language passages.
  • Example:
    • Bad: "You have " + n + " message" + (n > 1 ? "s" : "").
    • Good: ICU "{count, plural, one {# message} other {# messages}}".
  • Exceptions: Single-locale internal tools, still avoiding concatenation.

5. UX writing checklist#

  1. No placeholder text; sample data is realistic and labelled where it could mislead.
  2. Headlines are specific; no stock superlatives.
  3. Buttons are verb + object; dialogs repeat the action verb; links describe their destination.
  4. Errors say what happened and how to recover; empty states offer the next action.
  5. Sentence case and consistent terminology throughout.
  6. Strings are translatable (no concatenation), have room to grow and use Intl formatting.

title: Functioning implementation
description: Load when building UI in code: states, data flow, persistence and project boundaries.
html:
Load when building UI in code: states, data flow, persistence and project boundaries. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Build the whole relevant flow#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make the screen usable beyond its ideal state.
  • Reasoning: A decorative control or false success breaks trust.
  • Constraint: Implement relevant loading, empty, error, success, focus and disabled states. Await actual persistence or clipboard operations before success. Give recovery where possible. Preserve routes or redirects and existing behavior.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A copy button says Copied even when clipboard access fails.
    • Good: Await the clipboard promise and show manual-selection guidance on failure.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Keep state and response coherent#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Avoid jumping or stale UI during real use.
  • Reasoning: Repeated input, interruption and delayed responses expose optimistic assumptions.
  • Constraint: Handle rapid toggles, cancellation, stale responses and route changes. Keep layout stable while loading. Scope client state and effects; clean up observers/listeners. Profile before broad performance claims.
  • Example:
    • Bad: An old response overwrites a newer choice.
    • Good: Use request identity/cancellation as appropriate and retain only the current result.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Respect provenance and project boundaries#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Avoid unnecessary dependencies or unrelated edits.
  • Reasoning: A design task is not permission to replace unrelated work or publish.
  • Constraint: Inspect the workspace, review dependency source and licenses, preserve unrelated changes and stay within authorized deployment/push scope. Bundle one self-contained skill rather than hidden external rule dependencies.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Install an unreviewed remote script to create a static button.
    • Good: Use existing tools or a small local implementation after inspecting the project.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Conditional stack guidance
description: Load when the work touches a specific stack such as React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Tailwind or shadcn/ui.
html:
Load when the work touches a specific stack such as React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Tailwind or shadcn/ui. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Use the actual project#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Preserve existing functionality and conventions.
  • Reasoning: Changing frameworks is not a design improvement by itself.
  • Constraint: Inspect dependencies, architecture and project instructions first. Keep stack advice conditional. Use semantic HTML and native behavior regardless of framework. Review dependencies before executing install scripts.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Replace a working Vue product with Next.js for a visual refresh.
    • Good: Follow the existing component and route structure and verify affected flows.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Framework-specific implementation#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Use each stack intentionally.
  • Reasoning: Useful conventions depend on the project's version and architecture.
  • Constraint: In React use stable identities for changing lists; static immutable lists may use indexes. In Next.js keep server-first rendering and narrow client boundaries when applicable. In Vue and Svelte follow established project APIs and scoping. Use Tailwind tokens or arbitrary values when justified, not a categorical ban. Preserve primitive semantics when customizing shadcn or similar libraries.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Strip accessibility states while replacing a primitive's styles.
    • Good: Keep names, roles, focus and keyboard behavior while changing appearance.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Interaction and motion
description: Load when adding transitions, animation, gestures or any movement.
html:
Load when adding transitions, animation, gestures or any movement. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Decide whether to animate#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Make movement serve the task.
  • Reasoning: Frequency, purpose and interruption matter more than a universal duration cap.
  • Constraint: Ask what motion explains or confirms. Frequent actions often benefit from little or no animation. Choose timing from distance, size, purpose and frequency; evaluate the complete response, not just milliseconds. Springs and playful motion can fit. Do not decorate every keyboard action.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Replace a universal 400ms cap with a universal 300ms cap.
    • Good: Make a frequently used command palette immediate while a one-time teaching sequence takes the time it needs.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Handle interruption and origins#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Keep transitions connected to user control.
  • Reasoning: Rapid input exposes animations that restart, jump or block interaction.
  • Constraint: Retarget from the current state; support reversing and closing mid-transition. Use anchored origins for anchored overlays; centered dialogs may stay centered. Scope transitions to intended properties. Prefer simple transitions where suitable; use programmatic animation when behavior requires it.
  • Example:
    • Bad: An Escape action queues behind a drawer entrance.
    • Good: Escape closes from the drawer's current position and restores focus.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Gestures and reduced motion#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Support touch, keyboard and motion preferences.
  • Reasoning: Hover and drag are not available to everyone.
  • Constraint: Provide non-drag alternatives; use pointer capture and cancellation when dragging, ignore extra pointers as appropriate, and test interruption. Gate hover effects to suitable pointers. Respect reduced motion and preserve useful state feedback without compulsory movement.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A swipe-only destructive action or hover-only menu.
    • Good: An explicit action is available by keyboard and touch; drag is an enhancement.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Measure animation performance#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Avoid movement that harms interaction.
  • Reasoning: Transform and opacity are often cheaper, but acceleration is browser-dependent.
  • Constraint: Prefer suitable compositor-friendly properties; profile expensive blur, layout or large layers on representative devices. Do not claim every CSS animation or transform is GPU-accelerated.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Animate every paragraph with large blur during routine navigation.
    • Good: Keep content immediately available and inspect frame behavior under load.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Responsive behavior
description: Load when making layouts work across widths, zoom levels, touch and long content.
html:
Load when making layouts work across widths, zoom levels, touch and long content. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Break at content pressure#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Keep the important task usable at every width.
  • Reasoning: Device labels do not predict long strings, zoom or translations.
  • Constraint: Choose breakpoints when the composition needs them. Reorder only with a sensible reading and focus order. Inspect 320px reflow, small mobile and wide screens, long labels, zoom and landscape where relevant.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Keep four columns until labels break into letters.
    • Good: Collapse a grid once content no longer fits and retain the primary action.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Overflow deliberately#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Avoid clipping meaningful content.
  • Reasoning: Hiding overflow can conceal data, filenames and keyboard focus.
  • Constraint: Prevent page-level horizontal overflow. Allow scoped scrolling for intrinsically wide code/tables; give it accessible context and keyboard access when needed. Wrap filenames and prose when helpful. Do not hide essential content only to make a screenshot fit.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Ellipsize every skill filename with no way to read it.
    • Good: Wrap complete names and show the full path in a readable preview header.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Mobile navigation and touch#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep navigation reachable on small screens.
  • Reasoning: Desktop sticky sidebars can cover content when simply squeezed.
  • Constraint: Provide an operable disclosure or another suitable mobile pattern. Account for sticky header height in anchors. Verify touch-sized actions, no hover-only paths and no focus traps.
  • Example:
    • Bad: The current section falls behind a sticky header.
    • Good: Use one measured anchor offset and check it after resizing.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Accessibility
description: Load for every interface: keyboard, focus, semantics, names, contrast, targets and user preferences.
html:
Load for every interface: keyboard, focus, semantics, names, contrast, targets and user preferences. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Keyboard, focus and semantics#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Make core tasks operable and understandable.
  • Reasoning: Visual polish cannot replace operability.
  • Constraint: Use native semantics where possible, accessible names and sensible heading order. Preserve visible focus with sufficient contrast and no clipping. Support Enter/Space according to control semantics. Dialogs manage focus, Escape and return focus. Do not add positive tabindex to force an order.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A clickable div has no name or keyboard behavior.
    • Good: Use a named button with native activation and a visible focus indicator.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Targets and alternatives#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep actions reachable without precision or hover.
  • Reasoning: Small isolated targets and gesture-only actions exclude people.
  • Constraint: Use comfortably sized targets; 44px is a useful touch design target, not a blanket claim about every WCAG level. Evaluate applicable 24px target/spacing requirements and exceptions. Provide labels, non-color cues, non-drag alternatives and reachable mobile controls.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A tiny icon is the only way to dismiss an error.
    • Good: A named close action has adequate target area and can be reached with the keyboard.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Forms and feedback#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Explain input, progress and recovery.
  • Reasoning: Placeholders disappear; silent errors leave users guessing.
  • Constraint: Use persistent labels, descriptions where needed and errors associated with inputs. Announce appropriate status changes without repeatedly interrupting assistive technology. Report actual outcomes. Check reduced motion, zoom/reflow and image alternatives.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Announce success before a request finishes.
    • Good: Show progress, then confirmed success or a specific recoverable error.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Concrete patterns#

Page structure#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Let assistive technology users navigate by structure.
  • Reasoning: Screen-reader users jump by landmarks and headings; a page of divs is one long blob.
  • Constraint: One <h1> per page; headings in order without skipping levels for styling. Landmarks: <header>, <nav aria-label>, <main> (one), <aside>, <footer>. A "Skip to content" link as the first focusable element, visible on focus. lang on <html>. Unique, descriptive <title> per route; on client-side navigation, update the title and move focus to the new page heading or announce the change.
  • Exceptions: None.

Use native elements, then ARIA#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Get keyboard and screen-reader behaviour for free.
  • Reasoning: A div with a click handler is not focusable, not announced and does not respond to Enter or Space.
  • Constraint: Navigation is <a href>; actions are <button type="button">. Use <dialog> or an accessible primitive (Radix, React Aria, Headless UI, Ark) for dialogs, menus, comboboxes, tabs and listboxes rather than hand-rolling them. When building custom widgets, follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices pattern exactly (roles, states such as aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-controls, and the arrow-key model). No ARIA is better than wrong ARIA.
Widget Keys
Menu button Enter/Space/↓ opens, ↑↓ move, Enter selects, Escape closes and returns focus
Tabs ←→ move between tabs, Home/End, Tab moves into the panel
Dialog Focus moves in, Tab cycles inside, Escape closes, focus returns to the trigger
Combobox Type filters, ↑↓ move, Enter selects, Escape clears or closes
Disclosure/accordion Enter/Space toggles; heading wraps the button
  • Exceptions: None.

Focus that is always visible#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Show keyboard users where they are.
  • Reasoning: outline: none without a replacement makes keyboard use impossible.
  • Constraint: Style :focus-visible with a 2px ring at 3:1 contrast against both the component and the background, offset 2px so it is not clipped. Never remove focus styles. Ensure sticky headers and footers do not cover the focused element (scroll-padding-top). Support Windows High Contrast / forced-colors: active by using real borders or outlines rather than box-shadow alone for essential boundaries.
  • Exceptions: None.

Motion, zoom and preferences#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Respect user settings.
  • Reasoning: Vestibular disorders, low vision and cognitive load are common, and operating systems expose preferences for them.
  • Constraint: Honour prefers-reduced-motion (replace movement with fades or nothing), prefers-color-scheme, prefers-contrast: more where practical, and text zoom to 200% plus 400% reflow at 320 CSS px without loss of content. Use rem for font sizes so user font settings apply. Never disable pinch zoom (user-scalable=no). Auto-playing, moving content longer than 5 seconds needs pause.
  • Exceptions: None.

Accessibility checklist#

  1. Keyboard only: every action reachable, order logical, focus always visible, no traps.
  2. Landmarks, one h1, ordered headings, skip link, page titles.
  3. Every control has an accessible name; icon buttons included.
  4. Text 4.5:1, large text and UI boundaries 3:1, in every theme and over images.
  5. Errors linked to fields; status changes announced politely.
  6. Reduced motion, 200% text zoom, 320px reflow and forced colours checked.
  7. Automated scan (axe, Lighthouse) run and reported as partial evidence, not certification.

title: Frontend performance
description: Load when building pages that must feel fast, adding fonts, images, video, shaders or heavy client code, or when an audit reports slowness.
html:
Load when building pages that must feel fast, adding fonts, images, video, shaders or heavy client code, or when an audit reports slowness. Speed is part of the design: a beautiful page that shifts while loading or lags on input reads as broken. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. Targets#

Design to Core Web Vitals#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Give "fast" a measurable meaning.
  • Reasoning: Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds track what people perceive as loading, responsiveness and stability.
  • Constraint: Aim for "good" at the 75th percentile of real users: Largest Contentful Paint ≤ 2.5s, Interaction to Next Paint ≤ 200ms, Cumulative Layout Shift ≤ 0.1. Lab tools (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) diagnose; field data (CrUX, RUM) judges. State test conditions with any number you report and never present one local load as proof.
  • Exceptions: Internal tools on known hardware may set their own budgets; still avoid layout shift.

2. Loading (LCP)#

Make the hero arrive first#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Show the main content quickly.
  • Reasoning: The largest element is usually the hero image or headline; anything that delays it delays the page.
  • Constraint: Server-render or statically render above-the-fold content. Give the LCP image fetchpriority="high", no lazy loading, modern format, correct size; preload it if it is a CSS background. Do not hide the hero behind a JavaScript entrance animation that starts at opacity: 0 before hydration; animate from visible or use CSS that runs immediately. Defer non-critical scripts (defer, async, dynamic import), third-party widgets and chat bubbles until after load or interaction.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A headline revealed by a client-side animation library, invisible until 1.8MB of JavaScript hydrates.
    • Good: The headline renders in HTML and rises with a CSS animation; the shader canvas mounts after first paint.
  • Exceptions: None.

Load fonts without shifting or hiding text#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Avoid invisible text and layout jumps.
  • Reasoning: Web fonts block text or swap with different metrics, moving everything.
  • Constraint: Self-host fonts (or use the framework's font loader, such as next/font), use WOFF2, subset to the scripts you need, prefer one variable font over many static weights, and limit families to two. Use font-display: swap (or optional for non-critical faces) and a metric-matched fallback (size-adjust, ascent-override, or the framework's automatic fallback) to keep layout stable. Preload only the one or two files used above the fold.
  • Exceptions: System-font stacks need none of this.

3. Stability (CLS)#

Reserve space for everything#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Stop content from jumping under the reader's finger.
  • Reasoning: Shifts cause misclicks and look unfinished.
  • Constraint: Set dimensions or aspect-ratio on images, video, iframes, embeds and ads. Skeletons match final size. Never insert banners or cookie bars above existing content after load; overlay them or reserve their space. Animate with transform and opacity, not top, height or margin. Keep buttons the same width when their label changes to a spinner.
  • Exceptions: Changes in direct response to user input within 500ms do not count as shifts, but should still be smooth.

4. Responsiveness (INP)#

Keep the main thread free#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Respond to every tap and keypress within about 100–200ms.
  • Reasoning: Long tasks block input; heavy hydration makes buttons feel dead.
  • Constraint: Give visual feedback immediately, then do the work. Break tasks over 50ms (yield with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout, move work to a Web Worker). Debounce search and resize handlers; use passive scroll listeners. Virtualise lists beyond a few hundred rows. In React, keep client components small and leaf-level, use transitions (useTransition) for non-urgent updates, memoise expensive renders only after profiling. Avoid large client-side libraries for small jobs (a date library for one format, an animation library for a hover).
  • Exceptions: None.

5. Weight and effects#

Budget what ships#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Keep pages light on mid-range phones and slow networks.
  • Reasoning: Median mobile devices are several times slower than a developer laptop.
  • Constraint: Starting budgets for a landing page: under about 200KB compressed JavaScript, under about 1MB total transfer for the first view, one or two font files, hero image under about 200KB. Inspect the bundle (framework analyser) before adding dependencies. Tree-shake icon imports (import single icons, not the whole set).
  • Exceptions: Complex apps set per-route budgets.

Expensive visuals need a fallback#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep shaders, blurs and 3D from ruining the page.
  • Reasoning: WebGL, large backdrop-filter blurs and video backgrounds can drop frames, drain batteries and fail on some devices.
  • Constraint: Render a static image or gradient first and mount the shader/3D after load and only when visible (IntersectionObserver); pause when off-screen or the tab is hidden; respect prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-reduced-data where supported; cap device pixel ratio for canvases (about 1.5–2). Limit backdrop-filter to small, fixed elements. Profile on a throttled CPU before shipping.
  • Exceptions: None.

6. Performance checklist#

  1. Above-the-fold content renders without waiting for client JavaScript.
  2. LCP image prioritised; other images lazy, sized and in modern formats.
  3. Fonts self-hosted, subset, swap with metric-matched fallbacks.
  4. No layout shift from images, embeds, banners, fonts or loading states.
  5. Inputs respond within about 100ms; no long tasks during interaction.
  6. Heavy visuals have a static fallback, pause off-screen and respect reduced motion.
  7. Numbers reported with tool, device, network and lab/field context.

title: Avoid unconsidered defaults
description: Load when output risks looking generic, or when reviewing for unconsidered defaults.
html:
Load when output risks looking generic, or when reviewing for unconsidered defaults. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Question defaults, not vocabularies#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Preserve product-specific personality.
  • Reasoning: Banning a font, hue or familiar pattern does not create judgment.
  • Constraint: Poppins, purple gradients, cards, illustrations and familiar layouts are valid if considered. Inspect whether each choice serves the product, audience and content. Do not force neutrality or colorfulness.
  • Example:
    • Bad: All products use black/white, Inter, centered hero and three feature cards because it feels safe.
    • Good: A reading tool prioritizes text; a festival page may use expressive color and type.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Show something true#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Avoid fabricated proof.
  • Reasoning: A realistic-looking mockup can be mistaken for shipped results.
  • Constraint: Label illustrative samples, fictional data and concepts. Do not fabricate testimonials, ratings, customer logos, metrics or intentionally bad baselines. Keep claims and attribution accurate.
  • Example:
    • Bad: A hand-built comparison is presented as a measured model benchmark.
    • Good: A walkthrough says it is illustrative and lists what is untested.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Earn the decoration#

  • Confidence Level: Taste hypothesis
  • Purpose: Make visual details support the whole composition.
  • Reasoning: Removing personality is as automatic as adding unrelated filler.
  • Constraint: Choose a personality carrier deliberately. Ask whether a visual explains, guides or expresses something relevant. Decoration may be appropriate; remove it when it obscures content or delays frequent actions.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Add a random hardware chip to a Markdown design skill.
    • Good: Show an original brief-to-decisions-to-interface demonstration.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Common tells of unconsidered output#

None of these is banned. Each is a default that appears when nobody decided. If one is on the page, be able to say why it serves this product; otherwise replace it.

Tell Usually better
Purple-to-blue gradient on the headline, buttons and background at once One accent for actions; colour and gradient in the visual, not the text
Centred hero, three equal icon cards, logo strip, testimonial carousel, CTA band, in that order A composition chosen from the category playbook and landing composition
Emoji or generic icons in coloured circles as feature visuals Small real product fragments (visual craft §6)
"Unlock", "seamless", "revolutionize", "next-level", "all-in-one", "supercharge" A specific claim with a number or example (UX writing)
Glassmorphism, glow and noise on every surface One surface treatment, used where layering means something
rounded-2xl and shadow-lg on every element One radius family and elevation only where something floats
Inter at every size with weight 700 headings The chosen direction's type recipe, weight 500 display, size contrast
Fake logos, "10,000+ happy customers", five-star ratings without a source Real proof, or none, or clearly labelled samples
Dashboard of eight equal KPI tiles with sparklines Lead with the exception or decision (product UI)
Animated everything on scroll, bouncing buttons, parallax text Motion only where it explains or confirms (motion)
Dark mode made by inverting light mode Designed dark tokens (design tokens)
Lorem ipsum, "Feature one", "John Doe" Real copy and realistic sample data
Hand-drawn SVG "illustrations" of real objects Product UI, licensed photography or a generative field

title: Verify rendered results
description: Load before reporting work as done: rendered checks, measurement and honest evidence.
html:
Load before reporting work as done: rendered checks, measurement and honest evidence. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

Inspect, revise, repeat#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Check the actual interface against its direction.
  • Reasoning: Source review and a green build do not reveal every visual or interaction failure.
  • Constraint: Inspect desktop and small mobile renders in each supported theme. Exercise the primary task, states, keyboard, touch alternatives, anchors, copy, theme persistence and long content. Revisit hierarchy, proportions and assets. Record what was actually inspected and revise failures.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Call a build production-ready without opening its screens.
    • Good: Show actual screenshots, test interactions and list remaining limitations.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Measure and qualify#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Keep performance and accessibility claims honest.
  • Reasoning: One fast local load or a token contrast check is limited evidence.
  • Constraint: Measure contrast of actual text/UI pairs; test focus, names, reflow, reduced motion and loading. Check links, fonts/images, console errors and production output. Measure performance with stated conditions and distinguish lab from field data. Do not imply full WCAG certification from partial checks.
  • Example:
    • Bad: It feels fast, so advertise a performance score.
    • Good: Record device/browser, viewport, run conditions and measured metrics with limits.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

Evaluate the skill fairly#

  • Confidence Level: Pattern
  • Purpose: Improve judgment without rewarding extra polish.
  • Reasoning: Unequal assets, content or iteration budgets confound comparisons.
  • Constraint: Use fixed briefs for a data-heavy dashboard, expressive landing and personal portfolio. Compare current and candidate under comparable model, content, assets and iteration budgets; add a no-skill baseline when practical. Record revisions and failures. Score task clarity, composition, fit, distinctness, responsive behavior, accessibility, states and implementation. Investigate repeated templates. A few runs do not prove universal quality.
  • Example:
    • Bad: Compare a neglected baseline with a heavily revised candidate.
    • Good: Retain all outputs and revision budgets; report failures and unrun conditions.
  • Exceptions: Patterns may change when the product, user constraints or observed evidence justify it. Requirements remain.

title: Audit rubric
description: Load for /design-skill audit, design reviews, pre-launch checks and "why does this look off?" questions.
html:
Load for /design-skill audit, design reviews, pre-launch checks and "why does this look off?" questions. It turns the other references into one scored pass with a consistent report. Requirement = correctness/accessibility obligation; Pattern = adaptable starting point; Taste hypothesis = design judgment to validate in context.

1. How to audit#

Inspect the real thing#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Report observed issues, not guesses from source code.
  • Reasoning: Many failures (overflow, contrast over images, focus clipping, font fallback) only appear in a render.
  • Constraint: Render the interface at 1440px and 390px (plus 1024px for product UI), in each supported theme. Exercise the primary task with mouse, keyboard only and touch emulation. Trigger loading, empty, error and success states where possible. Read the source for semantics, tokens and states. Note what you could not inspect.
  • Exceptions: When only screenshots are available, say so and limit findings to what is visible.

Preserve intent#

  • Confidence Level: Requirement
  • Purpose: Improve the product without replacing its brand.
  • Reasoning: An audit that "fixes" a deliberate expressive direction into generic neutrality is a regression.
  • Constraint: Identify the intended direction first (see style directions). Judge against that direction and the product's audience, not against a personal default. Flag a direction mismatch as one finding rather than rewriting everything.
  • Exceptions: The user asks for a redesign.

2. What to score#

Score each area 0–3 (0 broken, 1 weak, 2 solid, 3 excellent) and list findings under it.

Area Look for Reference
Task clarity Primary action obvious; hierarchy leads the eye to it; nothing competes layout, product UI
Composition Proportions, alignment, rhythm, consistent spacing scale, narrow copy blocks visual craft, landing composition
Typography Family discipline, scale, measure, wraps, orphans, numerals typography
Colour and contrast Roles, accent restraint, measured contrast in both themes, no colour-only meaning color, tokens
Components and states Consistent controls, loading/empty/error/success/disabled present and truthful components, forms
Content Specific copy, verbs on buttons, helpful errors, no fabricated proof UX writing, anti-slop
Visual assets High-fidelity hero, consistent icons and images, licensed sources iconography and imagery
Accessibility Keyboard, focus, names, semantics, targets, reduced motion, zoom accessibility
Responsive 320–390px reflow, no horizontal overflow, mobile nav, touch targets responsive
Motion Purposeful, interruptible, fast for frequent actions, reduced-motion safe motion
Performance LCP element, layout shift, input delay, heavy assets performance
Distinctiveness Product-specific choices versus unconsidered defaults anti-slop, category playbook

3. Severity#

Severity Meaning Examples
Critical Blocks a task, excludes a group of users, or misleads Form cannot be submitted by keyboard; text fails 3:1; fake testimonials; page overflows at 390px hiding the CTA
Major Clearly harms usability, trust or perceived quality Missing error states; three button styles; hero visual is clip-art; body text 13px grey on grey
Minor Polish issues a careful user notices Uneven section padding; orphan word in headline; icon misaligned by 1px
Suggestion Optional improvements or taste calls Try the serif accent on one phrase; tighten the KPI strip

Mark each finding as measured (contrast ratio, computed size, observed overflow) or judgment (taste hypothesis), and never present a judgment as a measured failure.

4. Report format#

Return findings in this structure, most severe first:

## Summary
One paragraph: what the interface does well, the biggest problem, overall verdict.

## Scores
Task clarity 2 · Composition 1 · Typography 2 · Colour 3 · States 1 · Content 2 ·
Assets 1 · Accessibility 1 · Responsive 2 · Motion 3 · Performance 2 · Distinctiveness 1

## Findings
1. [Critical · measured] Primary button text fails contrast (2.8:1, needs 4.5:1)
   Where: hero "Start free trial", light theme
   Fix: darken --color-accent to oklch(0.50 0.19 262) (5.1:1), or use dark text.

2. [Major · judgment] Feature section is three identical icon cards
   Where: /#features
   Fix: replace icons with product fragments (the inbox row, the rule editor, the chart) per visual-craft §6.

## Not inspected
Screen reader output, physical touch device, slow-network loading.

Each fix names the specific change (token value, component, copy) rather than a principle. Offer to apply the fixes; group them so the most impactful land first.

5. Quick triage (five-minute pass)#

When time is short, check only these, in order:

  1. Can a keyboard user complete the primary task, with visible focus?
  2. Does any text or essential control fail contrast?
  3. Does anything overflow or hide at 390px?
  4. Is the primary action the most prominent element?
  5. Are loading, empty and error states present for the main data?
  6. Is anything fabricated (logos, testimonials, metrics)?
  7. Is there one obvious unconsidered default (identical cards, stock phrases, mixed icon sets)?
